title: Primary Care Approach to Care of the Elderly

topics.GIANT: Ageing in Malaysia & the 5 geriatric giants
topics.COG: Intellectual impairment: dementia, delirium, depression & cognitive tools
topics.WARGA: Warga Emas policies, programmes, institutional care & financial aid

cards.q: How is Malaysia's older population changing, according to DOSM estimates on the slides?
cards.a:
• Proportion aged **65 and above** rose from **8.0% (2025)** to **8.4% (2026)**
• Growth is **rapid** - elderly care is now a **healthcare priority**
• Aim is not just treating disease but keeping **independence, function and quality of life**
cards.m: 8.0 → 8.4: almost half a percentage point in one year

cards.q: What defines an 'aged nation', and when is Malaysia expected to become one?
cards.a:
• Aged nation = **15% of population aged ≥60** (or **14% aged ≥65**)
• Slide p48 (DWEN): expected by **2030** using the ≥60 definition
• Slide p4 (MOF citation): **2036-2048** depending on the definition used
• Note: the slides quote different years - learn the **15% / 14%** definitions, which are consistent

cards.q: At what age is a person classed as an older person (warga emas) in Malaysia?
cards.a:
• **60 years and above** (national policy, JKM and MOH definition)
• This is why JKM schemes (e.g. **Bantuan Warga Emas**, **Rumah Seri Kenangan**) require age **60+**
• WHO/Western literature often uses **65+** - do not confuse the two
cards.m: Malaysia: 60 is the magic number

cards.q: What approach to elderly care do the slides recommend in primary care?
cards.a:
• **Holistic**
• **Multidisciplinary**
• **Patient-centred**
• Goal: maintain **independence, function and quality of life**, not only cure disease
cards.m: HMP: Holistic, Multidisciplinary, Patient-centred

cards.q: What is meant by a geriatric syndrome ('geriatric giant')?
cards.a:
• Common health condition of older adults that **does not fit a single organ-based disease**
• Usually **multifactorial** (several small impairments add up)
• Major impact on **quality of life and disability**
cards.m: A giant has many feet - many causes, one presentation

cards.q: List the 5 geriatric giants (the 5 I's).
cards.a:
• **Immobility**
• **Incontinence**
• **Instability** (falls)
• **Intellectual impairment** (dementia, delirium, depression)
• **Iatrogenic** (drug-related) problems
cards.m: Can't Move, Can't Hold it, Can't Stand, Can't Think, Can't stop the drugs

cards.q: Why must a new geriatric giant (sudden fall, new confusion, new incontinence) prompt a search for acute illness?
cards.a:
• Older people often present **atypically** - e.g. pneumonia, UTI, MI or hypoglycaemia presenting as **confusion, falls, immobility or incontinence** rather than fever or pain
• The giant is the **final common pathway** of reduced physiological reserve
• Next step: full history, vitals, examination and targeted tests (urine dipstick, glucose, FBC, ECG)
cards.m: Off legs + off head = look for infection, drugs, metabolic

cards.q: Which members make up the multidisciplinary team caring for an older person from a Klinik Kesihatan?
cards.a:
• **FMS / medical officer** and nurses
• **Physiotherapist** (mobility, falls) and **occupational therapist** (ADL, home safety)
• **Pharmacist** (medication review)
• **Dietitian**, **medical social worker** (JKM schemes, abuse)
• **Caregivers / family** as core partners

cards.q: Define immobility in the elderly.
cards.a:
• **Impairment of the ability to move independently**
• Results in **limitation of life space**
• **Not a natural part of ageing** - always look for a cause
cards.m: Shrinking life space: town → house → room → bed

cards.q: What are the physical complications of immobility listed on the slides?
cards.a:
• **Muscle wasting**
• **Deep vein thrombosis**
• **Pneumonia and atelectasis**
• **Constipation**
• **Pressure ulcer**
cards.m: Clots, Chest, Colon, skin Crumbles, muscle Collapses

cards.q: Apart from physical problems, what social and mental complications does immobility cause?
cards.a:
• **Impaired quality of life**
• **Increased care burden** on family / caregivers
• Also social isolation and depression (lecturer addition)

cards.q: Which musculoskeletal conditions cause immobility in older adults?
cards.a:
• **Osteoarthritis**
• **Muscle weakness / sarcopenia**
• **Hip or lower limb fracture**
cards.m: Joints, muscle, bone

cards.q: Name the non-musculoskeletal causes of immobility shown on the slides, with examples.
cards.a:
• **Visual impairment**: cataract, glaucoma, retinopathy
• **Cognitive impairment**: confusion, depression, medication use
• **Neurological**: stroke, Parkinson's disease
• **Chronic disease**: CCF, COPD
• **Psychological**: fear of falling
cards.m: See, Think, Nerve, Heart-lung, Fear

cards.q: Why is fear of falling such an important cause of immobility?
cards.a:
• After a fall, the patient **restricts activity** to feel safe
• Less activity → **deconditioning, weakness, poor balance**
• Weakness → **more falls** → more fear (a vicious cycle)
• Break it with **physiotherapy, balance training, walking aids and reassurance**
cards.m: Fear → sit → weak → fall → more fear

cards.q: What are the first steps in managing an immobile older patient?
cards.a:
• **Explain and educate** patient and caregiver about the complications of prolonged bed rest and how to manage them
• **Manage the causes / risk factors** of immobility
• **Review medications** - reduce or stop drugs causing weakness or fatigue

cards.q: Which walking aids can be encouraged to improve mobility?
cards.a:
• **Walking stick**
• **Quad stick**
• **Walking frame**
• **Wheelchair**
• Choose by level of support needed; a physiotherapist should size and teach the aid
cards.m: Stick → quad → frame → wheels: more legs, more support

cards.q: What exercises are used in rehabilitation to restore functional independence in immobility?
cards.a:
• **Range of motion** exercise
• **Muscle strengthening** exercise
• **Balance training**
• **Gait training**
• Delivered via physiotherapy / rehabilitation
cards.m: RSBG: Range, Strength, Balance, Gait

cards.q: Why is nutritional and hydration support part of immobility management?
cards.a:
• Prevents **malnutrition**
• Prevents **anaemia**
• Prevents **electrolyte imbalance**
• Adequate protein also supports wound healing and muscle mass

cards.q: What DVT prophylaxis measure is listed for the immobile elderly patient?
cards.a:
• **Compression stockings**
• Plus early mobilisation and leg exercises
• Pharmacological prophylaxis (e.g. LMWH) is decided case by case when risk is high and bleeding risk acceptable

cards.q: How often should patients be repositioned to prevent pressure ulcers?
cards.a:
• **Bedbound**: every **2 hours**
• **Wheelchair-bound**: every **1 hour**
• **Able to self-reposition**: every **15 minutes** (shift weight)
cards.m: Bed 2, chair 1, self a quarter

cards.q: Apart from repositioning, what skin measures prevent pressure ulcers?
cards.a:
• **Moisturising lotion** (prevents dry, cracking skin)
• **Protective padding between extremities** (e.g. pillows between knees and ankles)
• Keep skin clean and dry, manage incontinence, optimise nutrition

cards.q: Which body sites are most prone to pressure ulcers?
cards.a:
• Lying supine: **sacrum, heels, occiput, scapulae**
• Lying on side: **greater trochanter, lateral malleolus**
• Sitting: **ischial tuberosities**
• All are bony prominences with thin soft-tissue cover
cards.m: Sit on ischium, lie on sacrum, heels always at risk

cards.q: How are pressure injuries staged?
cards.a:
• **Stage 1**: intact skin, **non-blanchable erythema**
• **Stage 2**: partial-thickness loss, shallow open ulcer or blister
• **Stage 3**: full-thickness skin loss, fat visible, no bone/tendon
• **Stage 4**: full-thickness with **exposed bone, tendon or muscle**
• **Unstageable** (base covered by slough/eschar) and **deep tissue injury**
cards.m: 1 red, 2 blister, 3 fat, 4 bone

cards.q: Which tool is used to assess pressure ulcer risk, and what score signals risk?
cards.a:
• **Braden scale** - 6 domains: sensory perception, moisture, activity, mobility, nutrition, friction/shear
• Score range **6-23**; **≤18 = at risk** (lower = higher risk)
• Re-assess regularly and on any change in condition
cards.m: Braden: low score, high risk

cards.q: What other complications of prolonged bed rest should you anticipate beyond those on the slide?
cards.a:
• **Deconditioning**: muscle strength falls roughly **1-1.5% per day** of strict bed rest
• **Joint contractures**
• **Orthostatic hypotension** on getting up
• **Bone loss** (immobilisation osteoporosis, hypercalciuria)
• **Urinary retention / UTI**, **delirium**, depression
cards.m: A week in bed can cost a month of rehab

cards.q: Define urinary incontinence.
cards.a:
• **Involuntary leakage of urine** caused by a **loss of bladder control**
• Common, under-reported and **not a normal part of ageing** - ask actively

cards.q: What symptoms may an older person with urinary incontinence report?
cards.a:
• **Involuntary leakage** of urine
• **Incomplete emptying** of the bladder
• **Constant dribbling**
• **Frequent urination** and **nocturia**
• **Sudden urge** to urinate

cards.q: List the risk factors for urinary incontinence.
cards.a:
• **Increased age**
• **Female** sex
• **Obesity**
• **Pregnancy** (and vaginal delivery)
• **Diabetes**
• **Smoking**
• **Family history**
cards.m: Old Fat Pregnant Female Diabetic Smoker with Family history

cards.q: What does the mnemonic DIAPPERS stand for in urinary incontinence?
cards.a:
Reversible (transient) causes:
• **D**elirium
• **I**nfection (UTI)
• **A**trophic urethritis / vaginitis
• **P**harmacological agents
• **P**sychological / physiological disorder
• **E**ndocrine (hyperglycaemia, hypercalcaemia → polyuria)
• **R**educed mobility
• **S**tool impaction
cards.m: Fix the DIAPPERS before buying diapers

cards.q: Which drugs commonly cause or worsen urinary incontinence in the elderly?
cards.a:
• **Diuretics** (furosemide) → polyuria, urgency
• **Anticholinergics, opioids, TCAs** → retention with **overflow**
• **Alpha-blockers** (prazosin) → urethral relaxation, **stress** leak in women
• **Sedatives / hypnotics** → reduced awareness, functional UI
• **ACE inhibitors** → cough provoking stress leak
cards.m: Water pills fill, anticholinergics block, alpha-blockers open the gate

cards.q: How does atrophic urethritis/vaginitis cause incontinence, and how is it treated?
cards.a:
• Post-menopausal **oestrogen deficiency** → thin, irritable urethral and vaginal mucosa
• Causes **urgency, frequency, dysuria** and recurrent UTI; reduces urethral seal
• Treat with **topical vaginal oestrogen**

cards.q: Stress incontinence: what is the pathology and classic presentation?
cards.a:
• Pathology: **pelvic floor muscle weakness** or **poor urethral sphincter function**
• Presentation: loss of **small amounts** of urine with **raised abdominal pressure** - coughing, sneezing, laughing, lifting, bending
cards.m: Stress = Sneeze

cards.q: Urge incontinence: what is the pathology and classic presentation?
cards.a:
• Pathology: **detrusor overactivity / instability**
• Presentation: **overwhelming need to pass urine** and **inability to control initiation** of voiding - often cannot reach the toilet in time
• Often with frequency and nocturia (overactive bladder)
cards.m: Urge = Unstable detrusor, gotta go NOW

cards.q: Overflow incontinence: what is the pathology and classic presentation?
cards.a:
• Pathology: **poor urinary stream / flaccid (underactive) bladder** due to **outlet obstruction** or **neuropathy**
• Presentation: **frequent involuntary dribbling** from inability to empty the bladder completely
• Exam may show a **palpable bladder**; PVR is high
cards.m: Overflow = a full bucket that spills

cards.q: Functional incontinence: what is the pathology and classic presentation?
cards.a:
• Pathology: **impaired mobility, cognition or environmental barriers**
• Presentation: **cannot reach or use the toilet in time** → leakage **despite normal bladder function**
• Management targets the barrier: commode, clothing, toilet access, prompted voiding
cards.m: Bladder fine - the journey fails

cards.q: What is mixed urinary incontinence?
cards.a:
• **Combination** of more than one type
• Most often **stress + urge** incontinence
• Treat the **predominant / most bothersome** component first

cards.q: What are the common causes of overflow incontinence in older men?
cards.a:
• **Benign prostatic hyperplasia** (outlet obstruction) - most common
• **Drugs**: anticholinergics, TCAs, opioids, decongestants
• **Faecal impaction**
• **Neuropathy**: diabetes, spinal cord disease, B12 deficiency

cards.q: What does the bladder (voiding) diary record, and for how long do the slides recommend it?
cards.a:
• Kept for **1 week** (slide)
• Records **fluid intake** (amount and type, e.g. caffeine), **voiding pattern** (times, volumes) and **leakage episodes with triggers**
• Helps classify the type and guides bladder training
cards.m: Diary of drinks, drains and drips

cards.q: Which physical examinations are done in an older patient with urinary incontinence?
cards.a:
• **Abdominal** examination (palpable bladder, masses)
• **Pelvic / gynaecological** (atrophy, prolapse) or **prostate** (DRE) examination
• **Neurological** examination (lower limb, perineal sensation)
• **Cough stress test** - leak on coughing supports stress UI

cards.q: Which investigations are done for urinary incontinence in primary care?
cards.a:
• **Urinalysis ± urine culture** (UTI, haematuria, glycosuria)
• **Blood glucose** (diabetes → polyuria)
• **Renal function**
• **Ultrasound for post-void residual (PVR)** volume
cards.m: Dip, sugar, kidneys, scan

cards.q: How do you interpret a post-void residual (PVR) volume?
cards.a:
• **< 50 mL**: normal emptying
• **50-200 mL**: borderline - repeat, review drugs
• **> 200 mL**: significant retention → suspect **overflow** (obstruction or underactive detrusor); refer urology
• Never start antimuscarinics in a patient with a high PVR
cards.m: Under 50 fine, over 200 refer

cards.q: What is the first-line management of urinary incontinence?
cards.a:
**Behavioural intervention**:
• **Lifestyle**: weight loss, smoking cessation, limit **caffeine and alcohol**
• **Pelvic floor exercises** (stress UI)
• **Bladder retraining** (urge UI)
• **Environmental modification**: home safety, bathroom access

cards.q: How are pelvic floor (Kegel) exercises prescribed for stress incontinence?
cards.a:
• **First-line** treatment for **stress** UI
• Slide: **3-5 contractions at least 3 times daily** → improvement in **50-80%**
• Standard guidance (NICE): **at least 8 contractions, 3 times a day, for at least 3 months** before judging response
• Note: slide's 3-5 contractions is lower than usual guidance
cards.m: Eight, three times a day, three months

cards.q: What is bladder retraining (bladder drill) and which type of incontinence is it for?
cards.a:
• For **urge incontinence** (overactive bladder)
• Patient voids by a **schedule**, resisting urges in between
• **Interval gradually increased** until continent for **3-4 hours**
• Usually for at least 6 weeks
cards.m: Drill the bladder to wait longer

cards.q: Which drug class is used for urge incontinence and for which type is it ineffective?
cards.a:
• **Anticholinergics / antimuscarinics**: **oxybutynin, tolterodine**, (imipramine - TCA with anticholinergic effect)
• Indication: **urge incontinence / overactive bladder**
• **Ineffective for stress incontinence**
• Combining drugs with **behavioural therapy** helps **60-75%**

cards.q: What are the side effects and cautions of anticholinergic bladder drugs?
cards.a:
• Side effects: **dry mouth, constipation, sedation, blurred vision, cognitive impairment**
• Contraindicated: **narrow-angle glaucoma**, urinary retention / high PVR, **severe constipation**
• Slide also lists **GERD** (a caution - they relax the lower oesophageal sphincter)
cards.m: Can't see, can't pee, can't spit, can't poo, can't think

cards.q: Why is oxybutynin a poor choice for an older patient with dementia and urge incontinence, and what is the alternative?
cards.a:
• Oxybutynin is highly **anticholinergic**, crosses the blood-brain barrier → **confusion, delirium, worsening dementia** (Beers list)
• It also antagonises **cholinesterase inhibitors** (donepezil)
• Alternative: **mirabegron** (β3-agonist; check BP - avoid in uncontrolled hypertension)
• Always optimise bladder training / prompted voiding first
cards.m: Donepezil + oxybutynin = foot on brake and accelerator

cards.q: When is surgery indicated for urinary incontinence and how effective is it?
cards.a:
• Reserved for **failure of conservative treatment**
• Effective in about **80%** of genuine stress incontinence
• Female stress UI: **bladder neck suspension** (suprapubic or vaginal approach) - in current practice the **mid-urethral sling** is the usual operation

cards.q: What surgical options exist for refractory urge incontinence and for overflow due to prostate enlargement?
cards.a:
• **Refractory urge**: **bladder augmentation** or **sacral nerve (root) neuromodulation** (also intravesical botulinum toxin)
• **Overflow in men (BPH)**: **TURP**, laser therapy or thermotherapy of the prostate

cards.q: What is the role of incontinence questionnaires?
cards.a:
• Validated tools to **screen** for incontinence and measure **symptoms** and **impact on QoL**
• **Not diagnostic** - abnormal results lead to further tests and evaluation
• Symptoms: **UDI, UDI-6**, Incontinence Severity Index, ICS male, Dan-PSS
• QoL impact: **IIQ, IIQ-7**, I-QOL, King's Health Questionnaire

cards.q: Describe the Urogenital Distress Inventory-6 (UDI-6) and its scoring.
cards.a:
• **6 core symptoms**: frequency, urge leakage, activity/stress leakage, cough/sneeze leakage, emptying difficulty, lower abdominal/genital pain
• Measures **symptom severity / distress** (developed in women)
• Score = **total ÷ 18 × 100** (range 0-100; higher = more distress)
• 0-19 minimal, 20-39 mild, 40-59 moderate, 60-79 severe, 80-100 very severe
cards.m: UDI-6: six items, divide by 18

cards.q: Describe the Incontinence Impact Questionnaire-7 (IIQ-7) and its scoring.
cards.a:
• Assesses **impact of UI on daily activities and emotional well-being**
• **4 domains**: physical activity, travel, social relationships, emotional health
• Score = **total ÷ 21 × 100** (0-100; higher = greater impact)
• 0-24 mild, 25-49 moderate, 50-74 severe, 75-100 very severe impact
cards.m: IIQ-7: seven items, divide by 21

cards.q: What is the QUID and how is it interpreted?
cards.a:
• **Questionnaire for Urinary Incontinence Diagnosis**: self-administered, **6 items**
• Distinguishes **stress (SUI)** from **urge (UUI)** incontinence in women
• **Q1-3** = stress score; **Q4-6** = urge score
• **Stress score ≥4 → SUI**; **urge score ≥6 → UUI**
• History remains the most critical diagnostic factor
cards.m: QUID: 4 for stress, 6 for urge (S before U, 4 before 6)

cards.q: How is functional incontinence managed in a patient with dementia or poor mobility?
cards.a:
• **Prompted / timed voiding** (caregiver offers toilet every 2-3 hours)
• **Bedside commode** or urinal, raised toilet seat, grab rails, clear path and night light
• **Easy-release clothing**
• Review sedatives and diuretic timing
• **Containment** products (pads) as adjunct, not first choice

cards.q: Why are long-term indwelling urinary catheters avoided in managing incontinence in the elderly?
cards.a:
• High risk of **catheter-associated UTI**, urosepsis, stones, urethral trauma
• Reduce mobility and dignity
• Reserve for **chronic retention** not amenable to treatment, non-healing **sacral pressure ulcer**, or palliative comfort
• Prefer **intermittent self-catheterisation** for retention when feasible

cards.q: How common are falls in older adults, according to the slides?
cards.a:
• Falls are the **leading cause of injury** in adults **≥65 years**
• **1 in 4** older adults report falling **every year** (over 14 million, CDC)
• Cause significant **morbidity and mortality**
cards.m: One in four, every year

cards.q: What are the consequences of a fall in an older person?
cards.a:
• **Physical**: fractures (hip, wrist), head injury, long-lie complications, death
• **Psychological**: **fear of falling**, loss of confidence, depression
• **Social**: reduced activity, isolation, institutionalisation

cards.q: List the non-modifiable risk factors for falls.
cards.a:
• **Age > 80**
• **Female** sex
• **Arthritis**
• **Cognitive impairment**
• **History of CVA or TIA**
• **History of falls**
• **History of fractures**

cards.q: List the modifiable risk factors for falls.
cards.a:
• **Environmental hazards**
• **Medication** (psychoactives, polypharmacy)
• **Metabolic** factors
• **Musculoskeletal**: gait, imbalance, weakness, pain
• **Neuropsychological** factors
• **Sensory impairment**: peripheral neuropathy, visual impairment
cards.m: HOME MEDS: Home hazards, Meds, Metabolic, Muscles, Mind, Senses

cards.q: What is the single strongest predictor of a future fall?
cards.a:
• A **previous fall** (especially recurrent falls)
• Every older patient should be asked **‘Have you fallen in the past year?’**
• Others: gait/balance impairment, fear of falling, fall-risk drugs
cards.m: The best predictor of a fall is a fall

cards.q: Which screening tools assess instability and fall risk?
cards.a:
• **Timed Up and Go (TUG)** - ≥12 s = increased falls risk
• **Berg Balance Scale** - balance and mobility
• **Morse Fall Scale** - mainly for inpatients

cards.q: When should an older person undergo further (multifactorial) falls evaluation?
cards.a:
• **≥ 2 falls** in the past year
• **1 fall + unsteadiness**
• **Difficulty with gait or balance**
• **A fall requiring medical attention**
cards.m: Two falls, one plus wobble, wobbly walk, or went to doctor

cards.q: What are the components of a multifactorial falls evaluation?
cards.a:
• **Full history** of the fall
• **Gait and balance** assessment
• **Vision and hearing** assessment
• **Orthostatic blood pressure** measurement
• **Home assessment**
(plus medication review, cognition, feet/footwear)

cards.q: What does a home hazard assessment look for?
cards.a:
• **Poor lighting**
• **Loose rugs / obstacles** / clutter / cables
• **Stairs** (rails)
• **Bathroom safety** (grab bars, non-slip mats, wet floors)
• **Appropriate footwear**
• **Suitability of walking aids**
cards.m: Light, Rugs, Stairs, Bathroom, Shoes, Sticks

cards.q: What does the AGS/BGS guideline recommend about falls screening?
cards.a:
• Screen **all adults aged ≥65 years** for fall risk **annually**
• Ask about falls in the past year and difficulty with walking or balance

cards.q: What are the four components of a falls risk assessment?
cards.a:
• **Falls history**
• **Medication review**
• **Physical examination**
• **Functional and environmental assessment**
cards.m: History, Drugs, Exam, Home

cards.q: Which past medical history items are relevant in a falls history?
cards.a:
• **DM, hypertension, epilepsy**
• **Previous falls**
• **Cardiac** and **neurological** history
• **Continence** state (rushing to toilet)
• **Vision**
• **Cognitive impairment**

cards.q: Which medications should be reviewed in an older person who falls?
cards.a:
• **Antihypertensives**, **alpha-blockers**, **diuretics**
• **Oral hypoglycaemic agents**
• **Psychoactive** drugs (benzodiazepines, antipsychotics, antidepressants)
• **Antiepileptics**, **analgesia** (opioids), **steroids**
• **Cholinesterase inhibitors**
• **Anticoagulants** (risk of bleeding if they fall)

cards.q: By what mechanism does each of these drug classes increase falls: alpha-blockers, sulfonylureas, benzodiazepines, cholinesterase inhibitors?
cards.a:
• **Alpha-blockers / antihypertensives / diuretics** → **postural hypotension** (diuretics also urgency, dehydration)
• **Sulfonylureas / insulin** → **hypoglycaemia**
• **Benzodiazepines, antipsychotics, opioids** → **sedation, slowed reaction, ataxia**
• **Cholinesterase inhibitors** → **bradycardia, syncope**
• **Steroids** → myopathy, osteoporosis (fracture if they fall)

cards.q: What should you ask about the period before the fall?
cards.a:
• Patient's view of the cause: **aware of impending fall** or **totally unexpected**; **trip or slip**
• **Premonitory symptoms**
• **Location and time** of day
• **Alone? What were they doing?**
• **General health** (infective symptoms, e.g. dysuria, cough, cellulitis)
• **Usual mobility** (independent, stick, frame, supervision)

cards.q: Which activity at the time of a fall points to which cause?
cards.a:
• **Getting up from lying/sitting** → **postural hypotension**
• **From the toilet** → **vasovagal** (micturition/defecation syncope)
• **In the middle of walking** → **arrhythmia**
• **Turning the head** → **carotid sinus hypersensitivity**
cards.m: Stand-postural, Toilet-vagal, Walking-heart, Turning-carotid

cards.q: Which premonitory or associated symptoms should be asked about before a fall, and what does each suggest?
cards.a:
• **Dizziness / light-headedness / vertigo** → postural hypotension, vestibular cause
• **Palpitations, chest pain, breathlessness** → **cardiac** (arrhythmia, ischaemia, aortic stenosis)
• **Sudden focal weakness, sensory loss, ataxia, confusion** → **stroke / TIA**
• **Aura** → **seizure**

cards.q: What does the patient's usual mobility tell you in a falls history?
cards.a:
• Whether they walk **independently** or need a **stick / frame / supervision**
• Dependence on aids implies **underlying frailty and poor mobility**
• Sets the baseline for rehabilitation goals

cards.q: What should you ask about during the fall?
cards.a:
• **Do they remember falling?** (amnesia suggests loss of consciousness)
• **Was it witnessed?** → take a detailed **collateral history**
• **Any loss of consciousness?** (syncope or seizure vs mechanical)
• Can they **describe the mechanism**?

cards.q: Which features after a fall suggest a seizure rather than syncope?
cards.a:
• **Limb jerking** (prolonged)
• **Urinary or faecal incontinence**
• **Post-ictal confusion** - not well-oriented after the fall, slow recovery
• Tongue biting (lateral)
• Syncope: brief LOC, rapid full recovery, pallor

cards.q: Why ask how long the patient was on the floor after a fall ('long lie')?
cards.a:
Lying > 1 hour risks:
• **Rhabdomyolysis** → AKI (check CK, renal function)
• **Pressure injury**
• **Hypothermia** and **dehydration**
• **Aspiration pneumonia**
• Strong predictor of **fear of falling** and loss of independence - consider a **personal alarm**
cards.m: Long lie: muscles break, skin breaks, temperature drops

cards.q: How is orthostatic (postural) hypotension diagnosed?
cards.a:
• Measure BP **supine** (after ~5 min lying) then **standing** at **1 and 3 minutes**
• Positive: **SBP fall ≥ 20 mmHg** or **DBP fall ≥ 10 mmHg** within **3 minutes** of standing
• Also note symptoms (dizziness) on standing

cards.q: Why examine the cardiovascular system in an older person who has fallen?
cards.a:
• To exclude **arrhythmia** (irregular pulse, bradycardia)
• **Valvular heart disease** - especially **aortic stenosis** (ejection systolic murmur, exertional syncope)
• **Heart failure**

cards.q: What does the musculoskeletal examination include in a falls assessment?
cards.a:
• **Footwear**: stability and grip
• **Remove footwear and examine the feet** (deformity, ulcers, nails, sensation)
• **Major joints**: deformity, instability, stiffness
• **Timed Up and Go test**

cards.q: What does the neurological examination aim to diagnose or exclude in a patient who falls?
cards.a:
Assess **muscle strength and tone, sensation, coordination and gait** to look for:
• **Stroke**
• **Parkinson's disease**
• **Myelopathy** (cervical spondylosis)
• **Cerebellar degeneration**
• **Cognitive impairment / dementia**
cards.m: SPMCC: Stroke, Parkinson's, Myelopathy, Cerebellum, Cognition

cards.q: Which blood tests are done after a fall and what is each looking for?
cards.a:
• **FBC** - anaemia, infection
• **Blood glucose** - hypoglycaemia
• **Renal function** - CKD, electrolyte imbalance (e.g. hyponatraemia)
• **Calcium and phosphate** - bone pathology
• **TFT** - thyroid dysfunction
• **Vitamin B12** - neurological abnormality (neuropathy, cognition)

cards.q: When are imaging and cardiac investigations indicated after a fall?
cards.a:
• **Spine X-ray, CT, MRI, EEG** - suspected neurological cause (or head/spinal injury, seizure)
• **ECG and echocardiogram** - suspected **cardiac** cause (syncope, murmur, arrhythmia)
• Holter monitoring for recurrent unexplained falls with suspected arrhythmia

cards.q: How is the Timed Up and Go (TUG) test performed?
cards.a:
• Patient sits in a chair, wearing **regular footwear**, may use their usual **walking aid**
• On 'go': **stand up, walk 3 metres** at normal pace, **turn, walk back and sit down**
• **Start timing when the patient stands up; stop when they sit back down**
• **Always stay by the patient** for safety
• Observe gait, stride length, sway and need for assistance
cards.m: Stand, 3 m, turn, return, sit

cards.q: How is the TUG result interpreted?
cards.a:
• **< 10 s**: normal mobility
• **10-20 s**: good mobility, independent
• **20-30 s**: mobility impairment, needs assistance
• **> 30 s**: high fall risk, dependent
• Fall-risk cut-off: **≥ 12 s = at risk of falls** (slides p12 and p32)
cards.m: Twelve seconds = take the fall-risk pathway

cards.q: What are the main components of falls management and prevention in the elderly?
cards.a:
1. **Acute medical management** - treat injuries, **taper/stop fall-risk-increasing drugs**
2. **Active physical rehabilitation and exercise**
3. **Targeted interventions** - environmental modification, **vitamin D**, treat underlying cause
4. **Walking aids** if gait is unsteady

cards.q: Which exercise interventions reduce falls in older people?
cards.a:
• **Progressive strength and balance training** (e.g. **Otago** home exercise programme)
• **Tai chi**
• Best when **individualised**, supervised by a physiotherapist, continued for **≥ 3 months**
• Walking alone is not enough for falls prevention in frail patients
cards.m: Strength + balance beats just walking

cards.q: What bone-health and targeted measures complement falls prevention?
cards.a:
• **Vitamin D** supplementation (about **800-1000 IU/day**) in deficient or housebound patients, with adequate calcium
• **Assess for osteoporosis** after a fragility fracture (DXA, FRAX) and treat (e.g. bisphosphonate)
• **Hip protectors** in nursing-home residents
• Treat cataract, postural hypotension, foot problems; review footwear

cards.q: How do the slides define intellectual impairment?
cards.a:
• A condition affecting **memory, thinking** and the **ability to perform daily activities**
• Results from a **variety of diseases affecting the brain**
• Affects **daily function** and **long-term care needs**

cards.q: What are the risk factors for intellectual impairment?
cards.a:
• **Non-modifiable**: **age > 65**, **female > male**, **genetic**
• **Modifiable**: **multiple comorbidities**, **psychiatric illness**, **traumatic head injury**, **social isolation**
• (Also hypertension, diabetes, smoking, hearing loss, physical inactivity)

cards.q: What are the three common cognitive problems in the elderly (the 3 Ds)?
cards.a:
• **Dementia** - chronic progressive decline in memory and acquired cognitive function
• **Delirium** - acute confusional state with disturbed **attention** and cognition
• **Depression** - can **mimic** cognitive decline
• They often **coexist** (dementia is the biggest risk factor for delirium)
cards.m: 3 Ds: Decline, Daze, Down

cards.q: What symptoms of intellectual impairment are listed on the slides?
cards.a:
• **Forgetfulness**
• **Lack of concentration**
• **Learning difficulties**
• **Reduced effective thinking**
• **Misjudging the spatial distance of objects** (visuospatial)

cards.q: How does DSM-5 define major neurocognitive disorder (dementia)?
cards.a:
• **Significant decline** from previous level in **≥ 1 cognitive domain** (memory, executive, attention, language, perceptual-motor, social cognition)
• Deficits **interfere with independence** in everyday activities (at least IADLs)
• **Not exclusively during delirium**, not better explained by another mental disorder (e.g. depression)
• Mild NCD = modest decline, independence preserved
cards.m: Decline + loss of independence + not delirium

cards.q: How do the slides define delirium?
cards.a:
• **Acute confusional state**
• Characterised by **disturbances in attention** and cognition
• (Develops over hours to days, **fluctuates**, usually has an underlying medical cause)

cards.q: How do you distinguish delirium from dementia?
cards.a:
• **Onset**: delirium **acute** (hours-days); dementia **insidious** (months-years)
• **Course**: delirium **fluctuates**; dementia slowly progressive
• **Attention**: **impaired early** in delirium; preserved in early dementia
• **Consciousness**: altered in delirium; clear in dementia
• **Reversibility**: delirium usually reversible once cause treated
cards.m: Delirium: Dramatic onset, Distractible, Drifting level

cards.q: What are the Confusion Assessment Method (CAM) criteria for delirium?
cards.a:
Delirium = **1 + 2** and **either 3 or 4**:
1. **Acute onset and fluctuating course**
2. **Inattention**
3. **Disorganised thinking**
4. **Altered level of consciousness**
cards.m: 1 and 2, plus 3 or 4

cards.q: What are the subtypes of delirium, and which is most often missed?
cards.a:
• **Hyperactive**: agitated, restless, hallucinating
• **Hypoactive**: drowsy, withdrawn, quiet - **most often missed**, worse prognosis; mistaken for depression or tiredness
• **Mixed**: alternates between the two
cards.m: The quiet patient can be the most confused

cards.q: What are the common precipitants of delirium in an older person?
cards.a:
**PINCH ME**:
• **P**ain
• **I**nfection (UTI, pneumonia)
• **N**utrition
• **C**onstipation (and urinary retention)
• **H**ydration (dehydration, electrolytes - hyponatraemia)
• **M**edication (anticholinergics, opioids, benzodiazepines) / alcohol withdrawal
• **E**nvironment change (hospitalisation, sensory deprivation)
cards.m: PINCH ME

cards.q: How should delirium be managed?
cards.a:
• **Find and treat the underlying cause** - this is the treatment
• **Non-drug measures first**: reorientation, family presence, glasses and hearing aids, sleep hygiene, hydration, mobilise, avoid restraints and unnecessary catheters
• **Low-dose haloperidol** only for severe agitation / distress or danger, short term
• **Avoid benzodiazepines** (except alcohol withdrawal)
• Note: slide lists antipsychotics as the delirium treatment; they are only a symptomatic last resort

cards.q: Which features suggest depression ('pseudodementia') rather than dementia?
cards.a:
• **Mood symptoms precede** cognitive complaints; relatively **rapid onset**
• Patient **complains of** poor memory (in dementia, family usually notices)
• **‘Don't know’** answers, poor effort; inconsistent deficits
• Past psychiatric history
• **Improves with antidepressant** treatment
cards.m: Depressed say ‘I don't know’; demented confabulate

cards.q: Which tool screens for depression in older people, and what is the cut-off?
cards.a:
• **Geriatric Depression Scale (GDS-15)** - 15 yes/no questions
• Score **≥ 5** suggests depression → full assessment
• Avoids somatic items that overlap with physical illness
• Always ask about **suicidal ideation** (older men are a high-risk group)

cards.q: On what is the diagnosis of dementia based?
cards.a:
• **Detailed history** (including collateral from family)
• **Physical and neurological examination**
• Supported by **cognitive, functional and behavioural assessment**
• Diagnostic criteria: **DSM-5**; severity staged by functional status

cards.q: What investigations are done in suspected dementia?
cards.a:
• **Baseline bloods**: FBC, renal function and electrolytes, LFT, **TFT**, **vitamin B12 / folate**, calcium, glucose, lipids; syphilis/HIV serology if at risk
• **Brain imaging**: **CT** or **MRI brain** (stroke, tumour, subdural haematoma, normal pressure hydrocephalus)
• **EEG** when seizures or rapidly progressive disease suspected

cards.q: Which potentially reversible causes must be excluded in an older person with cognitive decline?
cards.a:
• **Hypothyroidism**
• **Vitamin B12 deficiency**
• **Depression**
• **Drugs** (anticholinergics, benzodiazepines)
• **Normal pressure hydrocephalus** (gait apraxia + incontinence + dementia)
• **Chronic subdural haematoma**
• Neurosyphilis, hypercalcaemia
cards.m: NPH: Wet, Wobbly, Wacky

cards.q: What lifestyle modifications are recommended to protect cognition?
cards.a:
• **Regular physical activity**
• **Cognitively stimulating activities**
• **Active social life**
• **Smoking cessation**
• **Healthy diet**
• **Good sleep hygiene**
• **Educate caregivers** on management
cards.m: Move, think, mix, quit, eat, sleep, teach

cards.q: What drug treatment is used for dementia?
cards.a:
• **Acetylcholinesterase inhibitors (AChEI)**: **donepezil** (also rivastigmine, galantamine) - mild to moderate Alzheimer's disease
• **Memantine** (NMDA antagonist) - moderate to severe Alzheimer's or if AChEI not tolerated
• Started / supervised by specialist per **Malaysian CPG Management of Dementia (3rd ed, 2021)**; benefit is symptomatic, not curative

cards.q: What are the important side effects of cholinesterase inhibitors such as donepezil?
cards.a:
• **GI**: nausea, vomiting, diarrhoea, anorexia, weight loss
• **Bradycardia, heart block, syncope** → falls (check pulse/ECG before starting)
• **Urinary incontinence** - may trigger a **prescribing cascade** (oxybutynin added)
• Vivid dreams, insomnia (give in the morning if so)
cards.m: Cholinergic = SLUDGE + slow heart

cards.q: How should behavioural and psychological symptoms of dementia (BPSD) be managed?
cards.a:
• Look for triggers: **pain, constipation, infection, urinary retention, environment, caregiver approach**
• **Non-pharmacological first**: routine, music, activity, caregiver training, respite
• **Antipsychotics** only for severe distress or risk of harm, lowest dose, shortest time - they increase **stroke and mortality** in dementia
• Support and educate the **caregiver**

cards.q: Describe the Abbreviated Mental Test (AMT) and its cut-off.
cards.a:
• **10-item** quick bedside cognitive screen (age, time, address recall, year, place, recognise 2 people, date of birth, year of a national event, head of state, count 20→1)
• Each item 1 point, maximum **10**
• Score **≤ 7** (cut-off 7/8) suggests **cognitive impairment** → assess further
• Useful for delirium screening in acute settings
cards.m: AMT: 8 or more is great

cards.q: What is the structure of the Elderly Cognitive Assessment Questionnaire (ECAQ)?
cards.a:
• **10 items**, each worth **1 point** (maximum 10)
• 3 categories: **memory (3 items)**, **orientation (6 items)**, **memory recall (1 item)**
• Developed in Singapore for Asian elderly with **less educational bias**; used in **BSSK-WE** screening

cards.q: How is the ECAQ score interpreted?
cards.a:
• **7-10**: normal
• **5-6**: borderline cognitive impairment
• **0-4**: probable dementia → full assessment / referral
• Note: slide writes '>7 normal' and '<4 possible dementia', which leaves scores of 7 and 4 unclassified; the published bands are 7-10 / 5-6 / 0-4
cards.m: ECAQ: 7 up OK, 5-6 maybe, 4 down dementia

cards.q: What does the MMSE test and how are its 30 points distributed?
cards.a:
• **Orientation**: 10
• **Registration** (short-term memory retention): 3
• **Attention** (serial 7s / spell WORLD backwards): 5
• **Recall**: 3
• **Language** (naming, repetition, 3-stage command, reading, writing, copying): 9
• Used to detect impairment, grade severity and **monitor over time**; most used for **Alzheimer's disease** screening

cards.q: How is an MMSE score interpreted?
cards.a:
• Out of **30**; **< 24** generally suggests cognitive impairment
• Severity (commonly used bands): **21-26 mild**, **10-20 moderate**, **< 10 severe**
• Interpret in light of **education, literacy and language** - low education lowers scores; highly educated may score normally despite early dementia

cards.q: Describe the Montreal Cognitive Assessment (MoCA).
cards.a:
• **30-point** screen designed to detect **early / mild cognitive impairment**
• Takes about **10 minutes**
• **Add 1 point if ≤ 12 years of education**
• Domains: attention and concentration, **executive function**, memory, language, **visuoconstructional** skills, conceptual thinking, calculation, orientation

cards.q: How is the MoCA score interpreted?
cards.a:
• **26-30**: normal cognition
• **18-25**: mild cognitive impairment
• **10-17**: moderate cognitive impairment
• **< 10**: severe cognitive impairment
cards.m: MoCA 26 is the pass mark

cards.q: When would you choose the MoCA over the MMSE?
cards.a:
• **MoCA** is more **sensitive for mild cognitive impairment** - it tests **executive function and visuospatial** skills (clock, cube, trail-making) that the MMSE misses
• **MMSE** is widely used for Alzheimer's screening and monitoring severity, but has a **ceiling effect** in educated patients with early disease
• For low-literacy patients, the **ECAQ** or AMT may be fairer
cards.m: MoCA catches the mild; MMSE measures the obvious

cards.q: Define iatrogenesis in the elderly.
cards.a:
• **Illness or complications caused by medical treatment or interventions**
• Often from **polypharmacy**, **drug interactions** or **hospital stays**
cards.m: Iatros = doctor; genesis = origin

cards.q: What are the risk factors for iatrogenic harm in older people?
cards.a:
• **Drugs**: adverse effects even at **normal doses**; **polypharmacy**
• **Comorbidities**: multiple chronic diseases
• **Medical and surgical procedures**: invasive procedures
• **Investigations that are not indicated**
• **Prolonged hospitalisation**

cards.q: How is polypharmacy defined?
cards.a:
• Slide: **> 5 drugs**
• Most guidelines (WHO): regular use of **≥ 5 medications**; ≥ 10 = hyperpolypharmacy
• Risk of adverse drug reactions, interactions, falls and non-adherence rises with each extra drug
• Note: slide says >5; the usual definition is 5 or more
cards.m: Five fingers, five drugs - one hand full

cards.q: Why are older people more prone to adverse drug reactions?
cards.a:
• **Reduced renal clearance** (lower GFR even with normal creatinine) → accumulation (digoxin, gabapentin, sulfonylureas)
• **Reduced hepatic metabolism**
• **More body fat, less body water** → fat-soluble drugs (diazepam) last longer; water-soluble drugs reach higher levels
• **Lower albumin** → more free drug
• **Increased CNS sensitivity**, impaired baroreflex and homeostasis
cards.m: Less kidney, less liver, more fat, more sensitive brain

cards.q: Which CNS drugs are potentially inappropriate in the elderly and why?
cards.a:
• **Anticholinergics**
• **Antihistamines** (first-generation)
• **Sedatives** (benzodiazepines, Z-drugs)
• Risks: **delirium, cognitive decline, falls**

cards.q: Which cardiovascular drugs are potentially inappropriate in the elderly and why?
cards.a:
• **Alpha-blockers** (e.g. prazosin, doxazosin as antihypertensives)
• **Vasodilators**
• Risk: **orthostatic hypotension** → syncope, falls

cards.q: Which analgesics are potentially inappropriate in the elderly and why?
cards.a:
• **Opioids / meperidine (pethidine)** → **neurotoxicity** (pethidine's metabolite norpethidine accumulates → delirium, seizures)
• **NSAIDs** → **renal failure** and **GI bleeding** (also fluid retention, worsened heart failure and BP)
• Prefer **paracetamol** first-line; topical NSAIDs for localised OA

cards.q: What are the AGS Beers Criteria?
cards.a:
• **American Geriatrics Society Beers Criteria (2023 update)**
• A **medication review tool** listing drugs whose **risks outweigh benefits** in adults ≥65
• Used to guide prescribing and **deprescribing**

cards.q: Give the three categories of inappropriate drug use with the slide examples.
cards.a:
1. **Drugs generally to avoid** - e.g. **long-acting benzodiazepine (diazepam)** → falls, confusion
2. **Excess dosage** - e.g. **digoxin > 0.125 mg/day** for AF → toxicity due to reduced renal clearance
3. **Drug-disease interactions** - e.g. **NSAIDs in CKD or heart failure** → worsening renal function, fluid retention
cards.m: Avoid, Dose, Disease

cards.q: Why should digoxin doses in older people generally not exceed 0.125 mg/day?
cards.a:
• Digoxin is **renally cleared**; age-related fall in GFR → **accumulation**
• Narrow therapeutic index → **toxicity**: nausea, anorexia, confusion, visual (yellow-green) disturbance, bradyarrhythmias
• Higher doses add little benefit in AF / heart failure
• Toxicity worsened by **hypokalaemia** (diuretics)

cards.q: What are the STOPP/START criteria?
cards.a:
• European explicit criteria for older people
• **STOPP** = Screening Tool of Older Persons' **Prescriptions** - potentially inappropriate drugs to **stop**
• **START** = Screening Tool to Alert to Right Treatment - beneficial drugs that have been **omitted**
• Unlike Beers, START also tackles **under-prescribing**
cards.m: STOPP the harm, START the missing

cards.q: Give examples of START (omitted beneficial) medications in older people.
cards.a:
• **Anticoagulant** in AF (unless contraindicated)
• **Statin** in established cardiovascular disease (unless end of life)
• **ACE inhibitor** in heart failure or diabetic nephropathy
• **Vitamin D + calcium** / **bisphosphonate** in osteoporosis or after fragility fracture
• **Laxative** with regular opioids

cards.q: Why are first-generation antihistamines (e.g. chlorpheniramine, diphenhydramine) avoided in the elderly?
cards.a:
• Strongly **anticholinergic** and **sedating**
• Cause **confusion, delirium, falls, urinary retention, constipation, dry mouth**
• Often in cough / cold and sleep preparations
• Prefer **non-sedating** antihistamines (loratadine, cetirizine at reduced dose)

cards.q: Why is glibenclamide avoided in older patients with diabetes, and what is preferred?
cards.a:
• **Long-acting sulfonylurea** with active, renally cleared metabolites → **prolonged severe hypoglycaemia**
• Hypoglycaemia → falls, fractures, arrhythmia, confusion
• Prefer **metformin** (if eGFR allows), a short-acting sulfonylurea such as **gliclazide**, or a DPP-4 inhibitor
• Use **relaxed HbA1c targets** in frail elderly
cards.m: Gliben-CLAMPS the sugar too low for too long

cards.q: What is a prescribing cascade? Give examples.
cards.a:
• An **adverse drug effect is misread as a new condition** → a second drug is prescribed to treat it
• **Amlodipine** → ankle oedema → **furosemide** → incontinence, hypokalaemia
• **Donepezil** → urinary incontinence → **oxybutynin** → confusion
• **Metoclopramide** → parkinsonism → **levodopa**
• Always ask: could this new symptom be a drug side effect?
cards.m: New symptom? Suspect the last drug before adding a new one

cards.q: What are the key principles of safe prescribing in older adults?
cards.a:
• **Start low, go slow** - low starting dose, slow titration
• Clear indication for every drug; **review regularly**
• Adjust for **renal function** (eGFR / creatinine clearance)
• Simplify regimen (once-daily, blister packs, pill box)
• Avoid drugs on **Beers/STOPP** lists; check interactions
• Involve caregiver and pharmacist
cards.m: Start low, go slow, review, renal, simplify

cards.q: What strategies prevent and manage iatrogenesis in the elderly?
cards.a:
1. **Early recognition and treatment** of illness
2. **Close management of chronic illness**
3. **Routine medication review** - prescribe using **Beers criteria**, **deprescribe** unnecessary drugs
4. **Comprehensive Geriatric Assessment**
5. **Caregiver and patient education** - clear dosing instructions, explain side effects

cards.q: What is a Comprehensive Geriatric Assessment (CGA)?
cards.a:
• **Multidimensional, multidisciplinary** evaluation of an older person's **medical, psychosocial and functional** status (plus environment)
• Produces a **coordinated, individualised care plan** with follow-up
• Reduces institutionalisation and improves the chance of living at home

cards.q: What iatrogenic harms are linked to prolonged hospitalisation in older people?
cards.a:
• **Hospital-acquired delirium**
• **Hospital-acquired infections** including **catheter-associated UTI**
• **Deconditioning** and loss of ADL function
• **Falls** in an unfamiliar environment
• **Pressure injuries**, malnutrition, VTE
• Hence: **early mobilisation and early discharge planning**

cards.q: How is deprescribing carried out safely in primary care?
cards.a:
• **Brown-bag review**: patient brings all medicines, including OTC and traditional remedies
• Identify drugs with **no indication, harms > benefit**, or duplicates
• Prioritise, discuss goals with patient/family
• **Taper** drugs with withdrawal risk (**benzodiazepines**, antidepressants, beta-blockers, PPIs)
• Monitor for symptom recurrence and document
cards.m: Bag, Bin, Taper, Watch

cards.q: What are the goals of health screening in the elderly?
cards.a:
• **Detect disease early**
• **Prevent disability** and complications
• **Maintain independence**
• **Improve quality of life**
• **Promote healthy ageing**

cards.q: Which form is used for elderly health screening in Malaysian health clinics?
cards.a:
• **Borang Saringan Status Kesihatan Warga Emas (BSSK-WE)**
• Version **BSSK/WE/2008 Pindaan 1/2014**
• Two components: **health assessment** and **functional daily living assessment**
cards.m: BSSK-WE: the warga emas check-up form

cards.q: What does the health assessment component of BSSK-WE cover?
cards.a:
• **Sociodemographic** information
• **Past medical and surgical history**
• **Current health issues**
• **Dietary intake** and **oral health**
• **Physical activity**
• **Substance intake**: drugs, smoking, alcohol

cards.q: What does the functional assessment component of BSSK-WE cover?
cards.a:
• Screening for **risk of falls** and **gait impairment**
• **Mental health status** (cognition, depression)
• **Activities of daily living (ADL)**
• **History of abuse**
• **Physical examination** of all symptoms
• **Anthropometry** measurement

cards.q: What types of elder abuse should be screened for, and what do you do if it is suspected?
cards.a:
• Types: **physical, psychological/emotional, financial, sexual, neglect** (including self-neglect), abandonment
• Clues: unexplained bruises, delays in seeking care, poor hygiene, fearful patient, money disappearing
• Action: ensure safety, document carefully, involve **medical social worker** and refer to **JKM** / hospital **OSCC** as appropriate
cards.m: PPFSN: Physical, Psychological, Financial, Sexual, Neglect

cards.q: How is nutritional risk screened in older people?
cards.a:
• **Anthropometry**: weight, height, **BMI**, calf / mid-arm circumference
• **Unintentional weight loss** (> 5% in 6 months is significant)
• Tools: **Mini Nutritional Assessment - Short Form (MNA-SF)**
• Ask about **oral health / dentures**, swallowing, appetite, finances and who cooks

cards.q: Which other preventive checks should be offered to older people at a Klinik Kesihatan?
cards.a:
• **BP, glucose, lipids**, renal function in those at risk
• Cancer screening within age limits: **iFOBT** (colorectal), **mammogram**, Pap/HPV per programme
• **Vision and hearing** screening
• **Falls risk, cognition, mood**
• **Osteoporosis** risk assessment
• **Vaccinations**

cards.q: Which vaccines are recommended for older adults?
cards.a:
• **Influenza** - annually
• **Pneumococcal** (conjugate vaccine ± PPSV23) - especially ≥ 65 or with chronic disease
• **Herpes zoster** (recombinant) - prevents shingles and post-herpetic neuralgia
• **Tetanus (Td/Tdap)** booster - after injuries / every 10 years
• COVID-19 boosters as per national guidance
cards.m: Flu, Pneumo, Zoster, Tetanus: FPZT

cards.q: Why is screening of older people focused on function rather than only disease?
cards.a:
• Functional decline (ADL/IADL, mobility, cognition) predicts **hospitalisation, institutionalisation and death** better than diagnosis lists
• Many problems (falls, incontinence, hearing loss) are **under-reported** and seen as normal ageing
• Early detection allows **rehabilitation, aids and social support** to keep the person independent

cards.q: Which geriatric problems are typically under-reported by older patients and so must be asked about directly?
cards.a:
• **Urinary incontinence** (embarrassment)
• **Falls** (fear of losing independence)
• **Hearing loss** (thought to be normal ageing)
• **Memory problems** and **depression**
• **Elder abuse**
• Use direct questions and the BSSK-WE checklist

cards.q: Define frailty.
cards.a:
• An **ageing-related syndrome of physiological decline**
• Marked by **vulnerability to adverse outcomes**: **falls, disability, hospitalisation** (and death)
• Minor stressors (e.g. a UTI) cause disproportionate decline
cards.m: Frail = low reserve: small push, big fall

cards.q: What is the Clinical Frailty Scale (CFS) used for?
cards.a:
• A **well-validated** scale to quantify degree of frailty / disability
• Lets clinicians **screen for frailty and fitness** based on **clinical judgement** and evaluation
• Guides prognosis, intensity of treatment and advance care planning

cards.q: Describe CFS levels 1 to 3.
cards.a:
• **1 - Very fit**: robust, active, energetic, exercises regularly
• **2 - Fit / Well**: no active disease symptoms, exercises occasionally
• **3 - Managing well**: medical problems well controlled, not regularly active beyond routine walking

cards.q: What is CFS level 4?
cards.a:
• **Vulnerable** (version 2: **living with very mild frailty**)
• **Not dependent** on others for daily help
• But symptoms **limit activities**; commonly complain of being **slowed up** or tired during the day
cards.m: 4 = slowing down, still independent

cards.q: What is CFS level 5?
cards.a:
• **Mildly frail**
• More evident slowing; **needs help with high-order IADLs** - finances, transport, heavy housework, medications
• Progressive impairment of shopping, walking outside alone, meal preparation
cards.m: 5 = first help with IADLs

cards.q: How do CFS levels 6 and 7 differ?
cards.a:
• **6 - Moderately frail**: needs help with **all outside activities** and housekeeping; problems with stairs; needs help or prompting with **bathing**
• **7 - Severely frail**: **completely dependent for personal care** (physical or cognitive cause), but **stable** and not at high risk of dying within ~6 months

cards.q: What are CFS levels 8 and 9?
cards.a:
• **8 - Very severely frail**: completely dependent, **approaching end of life**; typically cannot recover even from minor illness
• **9 - Terminally ill**: **life expectancy < 6 months**, may **not be otherwise evidently frail** (e.g. advanced cancer)
cards.m: 9 = nine lives used up: terminal

cards.q: How should the CFS be scored when a patient presents acutely unwell?
cards.a:
• Score **baseline function about 2 weeks before** the acute illness
• Use history from patient **and** family/caregiver
• Designed for adults **≥ 65**; not validated in younger people or those with stable lifelong disability
• In dementia, the degree of frailty matches the degree of dementia

cards.q: What are the five criteria of the Fried frailty phenotype?
cards.a:
• **Unintentional weight loss** (≥ 4.5 kg or ≥ 5% in past year)
• **Self-reported exhaustion**
• **Weakness** (low grip strength)
• **Slow walking speed**
• **Low physical activity**
cards.m: Shrinking, Tired, Weak, Slow, Inactive

cards.q: How is the Fried frailty phenotype interpreted?
cards.a:
• **0 criteria**: robust (not frail)
• **1-2 criteria**: **pre-frail**
• **≥ 3 criteria**: **frail**
• Pre-frailty is the best window for intervention - it is often **reversible**
cards.m: 3 of 5 = frail

cards.q: How do frailty, disability and multimorbidity differ?
cards.a:
• **Frailty**: reduced physiological **reserve** → vulnerability to stressors
• **Disability**: **difficulty or dependence** in ADL/IADL
• **Multimorbidity**: ≥ 2 chronic diseases
• They overlap but are distinct - a person can be frail without disability, or multimorbid yet robust

cards.q: Which interventions can delay or reverse frailty in primary care?
cards.a:
• **Progressive resistance (strength) exercise** and balance training - most effective
• **Adequate protein and energy** intake; treat weight loss
• **Medication review / deprescribing**
• Correct **vitamin D** deficiency, treat anaemia, depression
• **Comprehensive Geriatric Assessment** and social support
cards.m: Move, Eat, Deprescribe

cards.q: What is the difference between basic ADL and instrumental ADL (IADL)?
cards.a:
• **Basic ADL**: self-care tasks - **feeding, bathing, dressing, toileting, transferring, continence**
• **IADL**: tasks for **independent living in the community** - shopping, cooking, housework, laundry, telephone, transport, medications, finances
• IADLs need more complex cognition and are **lost first**
cards.m: ADL = look after my body; IADL = look after my house

cards.q: What does the Lawton IADL scale assess?
cards.a:
• **8 domains**: using the **telephone**, **shopping**, **food preparation**, **housekeeping**, **laundry**, **transport**, **responsibility for own medications**, **handling finances**
• Scored 0-8 (higher = more independent)
• **Early decline** often signals early dementia or frailty, before basic ADLs fail
cards.m: Phone, Shop, Cook, Clean, Wash, Travel, Pills, Money

cards.q: What are the objectives of the Barthel Index?
cards.a:
• Assess a patient's **capability to perform daily activities**
• **Measure functional disability**
• Determine the **degree of assistance required**
• Total score categorises **dependency** from total to minimal assistance - informs **discharge and long-term care planning**

cards.q: In which settings and populations is the Barthel Index used?
cards.a:
• Both **inpatient and outpatient** settings; **monitors change in function over time**
• Most commonly used for **stroke** patients
• Also older adults, ICU patients, neuromuscular disorders, head injury, malignancy
• Typical places: hospitals, rehabilitation and stroke units, orthopaedic wards, long-term care facilities

cards.q: What are the 10 domains of the Barthel Index?
cards.a:
• **Feeding**
• **Bathing**
• **Grooming**
• **Dressing**
• **Bowel control**
• **Bladder control**
• **Toileting**
• **Chair (bed) transfer**
• **Ambulation** (mobility on level surfaces)
• **Stair climbing**
cards.m: Barthel's Ten: eat, wash, groom, dress, bowel, bladder, toilet, transfer, walk, stairs

cards.q: How is each Barthel Index domain scored?
cards.a:
• Each item scored from **0 (dependent)** upward according to degree of independence
• **Bathing and grooming: 0-1**; feeding, dressing, bowels, bladder, toileting, stairs: **0-2**; **transfers and mobility: 0-3**
• Total **0-20** (or ×5 = **0-100** version)
• Note: slide states every item ranges 0 to 1-2; transfers and mobility actually go up to 3

cards.q: How is the total Barthel Index score (100-point version) interpreted?
cards.a:
• **0-20**: total dependency
• **21-60**: severe dependency
• **61-90**: moderate dependency
• **91-99**: slight dependency
• **100**: independent
• A score of 100 does not mean the person can live alone safely - IADLs are not tested
cards.m: Barthel 100 = can do basic self-care, not necessarily live alone

cards.q: What is the Katz Index of Independence in ADL used for and how is it scored?
cards.a:
• Considered the **most appropriate instrument** to assess **functional status** - ability to perform ADLs independently
• Detects problems with ADLs and helps **plan care**
• Scored **yes/no (independent or not)** for each of **six functions** → total **0-6**

cards.q: What are the six functions of the Katz ADL index?
cards.a:
• **Bathing**
• **Dressing**
• **Toileting**
• **Transferring**
• **Continence**
• **Feeding**
cards.m: Katz is a DEFTTB cat: Dressing, Eating, Faeces/continence, Toileting, Transfer, Bathing

cards.q: How is the Katz ADL score interpreted?
cards.a:
• **6**: full function
• **4**: moderate impairment
• **≤ 2**: severe functional impairment
cards.m: 6 full, 4 moderate, 2 severe

cards.q: Compare the Barthel Index and the Katz Index.
cards.a:
• **Barthel**: **detailed** assessment, 10 domains, graded scores; tracks **finer changes in rehabilitation**; used in hospitals, rehab and stroke units, long-term care
• **Katz**: **quick screening** of basic ADLs only, 6 yes/no items; used in **primary care, CGA, community screening, nursing homes**
• Katz creates a common language and flags function to **prevent iatrogenesis**
cards.m: Katz = quick clinic check; Barthel = detailed rehab ruler

cards.q: In what order are activities of daily living typically lost and regained?
cards.a:
• Katz hierarchy: lost in order **bathing → dressing → toileting → transferring → continence → feeding**
• **Bathing is lost first, feeding last**; recovery happens in the **reverse** order
• IADLs (finances, medications, transport) decline even before basic ADLs
cards.m: First in the bath, last at the table

cards.q: What is presbycusis?
cards.a:
• **Sensorineural** hearing loss caused by **degeneration of the hearing organ** (cochlea) with age
• Most common cause of hearing loss in adults **> 55 years**
cards.m: Presby = old, acusis = hearing

cards.q: What are the typical features of presbycusis?
cards.a:
• **Gradual** onset
• **Bilateral and symmetrical**
• Affects **high frequencies** (high-pitched sounds, consonants) first
• **Men** have greater loss and earlier onset than women
• Difficulty hearing **in noisy places** and understanding speech
cards.m: Old ears lose the high notes first

cards.q: What should the clinical evaluation of hearing loss in an older adult include?
cards.a:
• **History**: risk factors, especially **noise exposure** and **ototoxic medications**
• **Examination**: otoscopy of the **auditory canal and tympanic membrane** for conductive causes (wax, effusion, perforation)
• Tuning fork tests (Rinne, Weber) to separate conductive from sensorineural
• **Gold standard: pure-tone audiogram**

cards.q: Which drugs are ototoxic?
cards.a:
• **Aminoglycosides** (gentamicin, streptomycin)
• **Loop diuretics** (high-dose IV furosemide)
• **Platinum chemotherapy** (cisplatin)
• **High-dose salicylates** (aspirin) - often reversible tinnitus
• **Quinine** / antimalarials
cards.m: A Loop of Cis-Aspirin-Quinine

cards.q: What is the gold standard test for hearing loss and what pattern does presbycusis show?
cards.a:
• **Standard (pure-tone) audiogram**
• Presbycusis: **bilateral, symmetrical, down-sloping high-frequency sensorineural loss**
• Air and bone conduction both reduced with **no air-bone gap**

cards.q: Which hearing presentation in older adults needs urgent referral?
cards.a:
• **Idiopathic sudden sensorineural hearing loss** (loss over ≤ 72 hours, usually one ear)
• Refer **urgently to ENT** - early **corticosteroids** improve recovery
• Also refer: unilateral or asymmetric loss (exclude vestibular schwannoma), associated focal neurology, painful discharging ear
cards.m: Sudden deafness = ENT emergency

cards.q: How is hearing impairment managed in older adults?
cards.a:
• **Treat underlying causes**: remove obstructions such as **cerumen (wax)**, stop or adjust **ototoxic medications**
• **Residual hearing**: **hearing aids**, **assistive listening devices**, rehabilitation programmes
• **Surgical implants** (e.g. cochlear implant) for severe loss

cards.q: When and how should older adults be screened for hearing loss?
cards.a:
• Recommended in adults **older than 50-60 years**
• **HHIE-S questionnaire** - perceived social and emotional effects of hearing loss
• **Whisper test**: stand **arm's length (about 60 cm) behind** the patient, mask the other ear by rubbing the tragus, whisper 3 numbers/letters; failure = inability to repeat most of them

cards.q: How is the HHIE-S scored and interpreted?
cards.a:
• **10 questions**, answers **yes (4) / sometimes (2) / no (0)** → total **0-40**
• **0-8**: no handicap, no referral
• **10-24**: mild to moderate handicap
• **26-40**: significant / severe handicap → **refer to audiologist**
• Score **≥ 10** = screen positive
cards.m: HHIE-S: 10 questions, 10 points positive

cards.q: Why do many older adults with hearing loss not receive treatment?
cards.a:
• **Failure to recognise** the loss
• Viewing it as a **normal part of ageing** or believing it **cannot be treated**
• **Non-adherence with hearing aids**: stigma, cost, inconvenience, disappointing initial results

cards.q: Why does sensory impairment matter so much in older people?
cards.a:
• **Hearing loss**: social isolation, depression, and it is the largest **modifiable risk factor for dementia** in mid-life (Lancet Commission)
• **Visual impairment**: **falls**, fractures, loss of driving, reduced ADL
• Both can **mimic or worsen confusion** and **delirium** - always provide glasses and hearing aids

cards.q: What are the key points on visual impairment in the elderly from the slides?
cards.a:
• **Blindness prevalence** rises in those **> 70 years**
• Commonly **asymptomatic in the early stage**
• **Screening every 12 months**
cards.m: Eyes once a year after 60

cards.q: What are the common visual problems in the elderly?
cards.a:
• **Cataract**
• **Refractive error** (long/short-sightedness, presbyopia)
• **Glaucoma**
• **Retinal detachment**
• **Age-related macular degeneration**
• **Diabetic retinopathy**
• Note: slide writes 'retinal displacement'; the correct term is retinal detachment

cards.q: Which eye examinations are used to screen older adults?
cards.a:
• **Visual acuity** (Snellen chart, pinhole)
• **Visual field** (confrontation)
• **Colour vision**
• **RAPD** (relative afferent pupillary defect - optic nerve disease)
• **Light brightness**
• **Ophthalmoscopy** (red reflex, disc, retina)
• **Intraocular pressure** (IOP)

cards.q: How do cataract, primary open-angle glaucoma and age-related macular degeneration present differently?
cards.a:
• **Cataract**: gradual **blurred / cloudy vision**, glare at night, **reduced red reflex**; vision improves with surgery
• **Open-angle glaucoma**: painless, **peripheral field loss** first (tunnel vision), **cupped disc**, raised IOP
• **AMD**: **central vision loss**, distortion (straight lines wavy on Amsler grid), drusen; wet AMD sudden → urgent referral
cards.m: Cataract = cloudy, Glaucoma = tunnel, AMD = central hole

cards.q: What is the role of the primary care doctor in diabetic eye screening of older patients?
cards.a:
• **Annual fundus screening** (fundus camera / dilated ophthalmoscopy) for all with type 2 diabetes from diagnosis
• Refer to ophthalmology for **sight-threatening retinopathy** (pre-proliferative or proliferative, maculopathy)
• **Sudden visual loss** in a diabetic (vitreous haemorrhage, retinal detachment) → same-day referral
• Optimise glucose, BP and lipids

cards.q: What is the Dasar Warga Emas Negara (DWEN)?
cards.a:
• National Older Persons Policy, **established 1995, revised 2011**
• **Vision**: elderly who are **independent, dignified and respected**
• Key objective: **empower individuals, families and communities** to face ageing

cards.q: What are the six strategies of the DWEN?
cards.a:
• **Honour and dignity**
• **Self-reliance**
• **Participation**
• **Care and protection**
• **Research and development**
• **Action plan**
cards.m: HSP-CRA: Honour, Self, Participate, Care, Research, Action

cards.q: What is the Pelan Tindakan Warga Emas Negara (PTWEN) 2026-2030?
cards.a:
• National Older Persons Action Plan - translates the **DWEN** into **actionable implementation**
• **Launched 5 October 2025**, replacing the expired **PTWEN 2010-2020**
• Target: **50,000 skilled elderly caregivers by 2030**

cards.q: What are the National Ageing Blueprint (NAB) and the RUU Warga Emas?
cards.a:
• **NAB 2025-2045**: White Paper to be tabled 2026-2027; **5 thrusts** - macroeconomics and fiscal policy, education and skills, **lifelong health**, **social protection**, **long-term care**
• **RUU Warga Emas** (Older Persons Bill): draft completed June 2025, expected in Parliament 2026; **human-rights based**, protects elderly from **neglect and abuse** - Malaysia currently has **no dedicated elderly law**

cards.q: What does the Care Centres Act 1993 (Act 506) regulate?
cards.a:
• **Registration, control and inspection** of all **care centres** - for elderly, disabled and children
• Requires **trained carers**, adequate **facilities** and **safety compliance**
• **Amended 2018** to strengthen provisions
• Advise families to choose a **registered** care centre

cards.q: What is PAWE?
cards.a:
• **Pusat Aktiviti Warga Emas** - **JKM** community centres promoting **healthy, active ageing**
• **217 centres**, about **49,000 active members** (Feb 2026)
• **Free** for all elderly members
• Funding: RM100,000 one-off establishment grant + RM50,000 annual operating grant per centre
cards.m: PAWE = JKM day activity centre

cards.q: What is KOSPEN Warga Emas?
cards.a:
• **KKM (MOH)** programme for **NCD prevention at community level**
• **Trained volunteers** monitor **BP, glucose and BMI**
• Conducts **health screening and fitness activities**
• Collaborates with **PAWE** for elderly exercise programmes

cards.q: What are Kelab Warga Emas (KWE) and Khidmat Bantu di Rumah (KBDR)?
cards.a:
• **KWE**: elderly clubs encouraging **community and NGO involvement** - **233 clubs under health clinics** (2017)
• **KBDR**: **volunteer home-help** for elderly **living alone** - meal preparation, bathing, housekeeping, companionship, medication support, hospital visits (~1,000 volunteers serving 5,000 elderly)
cards.m: KWE = club at the clinic; KBDR = help at home

cards.q: How do Rumah Seri Kenangan and Rumah Ehsan differ?
cards.a:
• Both are **JKM residential homes** for poor elderly **aged 60+** without heirs or income
• **Rumah Seri Kenangan (RSK)**: residents **able to self-care**, free from infectious / psychiatric disease
• **Rumah Ehsan**: **frail, unable to self-care**, **certified chronically ill** by a government medical officer
cards.m: Seri Kenangan = Self-caring; Ehsan = Extra care

cards.q: What is Bantuan Warga Emas (BWE) and who is eligible?
cards.a:
• **JKM monthly cash assistance** for poor elderly - increased from **RM500 to RM600/month** (2025)
• Eligibility: **aged 60+**, household income **below the poverty line (< RM2,589/month)**, **not in an institution**, not receiving other assistance
• Over 160,000 recipients
cards.m: BWE: 60 years, RM600

cards.q: What are mySalam and SMUE?
cards.a:
• **mySalam**: national **takaful** protection for the **B40** group - expanded from **45 to 50 critical illnesses** (April 2025); most common claim **cancer**
• **SMUE (Skim Mesra Usia Emas)**: Selangor scheme - **RM150 annual shopping voucher** + **RM2,500 funeral aid** (Khairat Darul Ehsan)

cards.q: What does PEKA B40 offer and who is eligible?
cards.a:
• **Free health screening** for **B40 individuals aged 40+** (STR recipients automatically eligible)
• Covers physical examination, breast/prostate screening, blood tests (glucose, cholesterol, renal), urine test, **mental health screening**
• **Medical device aid up to RM20,000** (e.g. hearing aids, walking aids)

cards.q: How can a primary care doctor link an older patient to social support in Malaysia?
cards.a:
• Identify needs during BSSK-WE / CGA (financial, caregiver, housing, abuse)
• Refer to the **medical social worker** / **JKM** for BWE, RSK / Rumah Ehsan, KBDR
• Encourage **PAWE**, **KWE** and **KOSPEN Warga Emas** for active ageing
• Check eligibility for **PEKA B40** and **mySalam**

cards.q: What does Surah al-Isra' (17:23) teach about the care of older people?
cards.a:
• Honour parents; when they reach **old age**, never say even **‘ugh’** to them nor yell, but **speak respectfully**
• Application: treat older patients with **patience, respect and dignity**, especially when frail, dependent or needing repeated help
• Care should include **respectful communication and emotional support**, not just medical treatment

cards.q: Which findings in an older person who has fallen need same-day referral to hospital rather than KK follow-up?
cards.a:
• **Head injury on an anticoagulant or antiplatelet**, or new confusion / vomiting / reduced GCS → urgent **CT brain** (subdural risk)
• Suspected **hip fracture**: unable to weight-bear, **shortened, externally rotated leg**
• **Long lie** with suspected **rhabdomyolysis**, hypothermia or pressure injury
• Fall with **syncope plus cardiac features** (exertional, palpitations, murmur, abnormal ECG) or new **focal neurology**
• Acute illness (sepsis) or unsafe to go home
cards.m: Bleed, Break, Long lie, Heart/Brain - 'BBLH' = send today

mcq.stem:
An 82-year-old woman is brought to the Klinik Kesihatan by her daughter. Over 2 days she has become muddled, fell once at home without injury, and has wet herself twice. She has no cough or fever. BP 128/76 mmHg, pulse 98/min, temperature 37.2 °C. She was fully independent last week.
What is the most appropriate next step?
o: Arrange an outpatient CT brain to look for vascular dementia
Start low-dose haloperidol at night to settle her confusion
Search for an acute precipitant: urine dipstick, glucose, examination
Start oxybutynin for her new-onset urinary incontinence
Refer for routine physiotherapy review of her fall next month
mcq.e: Several geriatric giants appearing together over days (confusion, a fall, incontinence) are an atypical presentation of acute illness such as UTI, pneumonia, hypoglycaemia or drug toxicity. The first job is to find and treat the precipitant. Treating each giant separately with drugs or delayed referrals misses the cause.
w: Wrong - an acute 2-day change is not dementia; imaging is not the first step
Wrong - antipsychotics do not treat the cause and add sedation and fall risk
Correct - acute multiple giants signal an underlying illness that must be found first
Wrong - oxybutynin is anticholinergic and would worsen confusion; the incontinence is likely transient
Wrong - delaying assessment risks missing sepsis or another treatable cause

mcq.stem:
An 85-year-old man is bedbound at home after a dense left hemiparetic stroke. He cannot turn himself. His wife, the main caregiver, asks how often she should change his position to prevent pressure sores.
What interval should you advise?
mcq.e: Bedbound patients who cannot move themselves should be repositioned every 2 hours. Wheelchair-bound patients need repositioning every hour, and those able to shift their own weight should do so about every 15 minutes. Longer intervals allow ischaemia over bony prominences.
w: Correct - 2-hourly turning is the standard for bedbound patients
Wrong - 4 hours is too long; ischaemic damage can begin within 2 hours
Wrong - 15-minute weight shifts apply to patients able to reposition themselves
Wrong - hourly repositioning is the interval for wheelchair-bound patients
Wrong - turning once per shift guarantees pressure injury over the sacrum and heels

mcq.stem:
An 80-year-old woman with advanced dementia now spends most of the day in a wheelchair at a care centre. She cannot lift or shift her own weight. The staff ask how often they should reposition her while she is seated.
What interval is recommended?
mcq.e: Seated pressure over the ischial tuberosities is concentrated on a small area, so wheelchair-bound patients need repositioning every hour, more often than bedbound patients (every 2 hours). Fifteen-minute weight shifts are for patients who can do it themselves.
w: Wrong - 15-minute shifts are for patients able to self-reposition
Wrong - 2 hours is the bedbound interval; sitting loads a smaller area
Wrong - 4 hours is far too long for any immobile patient
Wrong - not the recommended interval for staff-assisted repositioning
Correct - wheelchair-bound patients should be repositioned hourly

mcq.stem:
A 79-year-old man has been largely bedbound at home for 3 weeks after pneumonia. His daughter notices his right calf is swollen. The calf is 3 cm larger than the left, warm, with pitting oedema and mild tenderness along the deep veins. There is no fever and no skin break.
What is the most likely diagnosis?
mcq.e: Immobility is a major risk factor for deep vein thrombosis. Unilateral calf swelling over 3 cm, pitting oedema and tenderness along the deep veins score highly on the Wells criteria. Arrange urgent compression ultrasound. Cellulitis usually has fever, spreading erythema and a skin portal of entry.
w: Wrong - no fever, spreading erythema or skin break to suggest infection
Correct - immobile patient with unilateral swollen tender calf: DVT until proven otherwise
Wrong - possible, but there is no history of knee swelling or sudden calf pain
Wrong - lymphoedema is chronic, non-tender and develops over months
Wrong - heart failure gives bilateral oedema, not a single swollen tender calf

mcq.stem:
A district nurse reviews an 88-year-old bedbound woman. Over the sacrum there is a 3 cm ulcer with full-thickness skin loss. Subcutaneous fat is visible in the base, but no bone, tendon or muscle is exposed, and the base is not covered by slough.
What stage is this pressure injury?
mcq.e: Stage 3 is full-thickness skin loss with visible fat but no exposed bone, tendon or muscle. Stage 2 is partial-thickness (blister or shallow ulcer), stage 4 exposes deeper structures, and unstageable means the base is hidden by slough or eschar.
w: Wrong - stage 2 is partial-thickness only; fat is not visible
Wrong - stage 4 requires exposed bone, tendon or muscle
Wrong - the base is visible, so it can be staged
Correct - full-thickness loss with fat visible and no deeper exposure
Wrong - deep tissue injury is intact skin with purple or maroon discolouration

mcq.stem:
An 84-year-old woman with bilateral knee osteoarthritis has gradually stopped leaving her house. She now walks slowly holding on to furniture, has weak quadriceps and poor balance, but no acute pain flare. Her X-rays show moderate OA. She wants to walk to the surau again.
What is the most appropriate management to improve her mobility?
o: Advise strict rest until the knees feel less stiff
Physiotherapy for strength, balance and gait with a walking aid
Prescribe diazepam at night to relieve muscle stiffness
Order an MRI of both knees before starting any exercise
Provide a wheelchair for all mobility outside the home
mcq.e: Immobility is not normal ageing and worsens with rest. Rehabilitation with range-of-motion, strengthening, balance and gait training plus an appropriate walking aid restores function. Rest, sedatives and premature wheelchair use accelerate deconditioning.
w: Wrong - rest causes further muscle wasting and stiffness
Correct - targeted physiotherapy plus a walking aid restores functional independence
Wrong - benzodiazepines cause sedation and falls in the elderly
Wrong - imaging adds nothing; exercise is safe and indicated in OA
Wrong - a wheelchair would remove remaining walking ability and accelerate decline

mcq.stem:
An 81-year-old man has become increasingly drowsy and weak over 2 months and now spends most of the day in bed. Six weeks ago amitriptyline was increased to 50 mg at night for diabetic neuropathic pain. Examination shows no focal neurology. Glucose and electrolytes are normal.
What is the best first step to improve his mobility?
o: Start a high-protein supplement and review in 3 months
