Refer for a walking frame and home physiotherapy only
Arrange a CT brain to exclude a silent stroke
Reduce and then stop the amitriptyline, then reassess
Add modafinil in the morning to counter his drowsiness
mcq.e: Medication review is part of immobility management: reduce or stop drugs that cause weakness, fatigue or sedation. Amitriptyline is sedating and anticholinergic and is a Beers-list drug in older adults. Adding another drug to counter a side effect is a prescribing cascade.
w: Wrong - nutrition helps but does not address the cause of his sedation
Wrong - rehabilitation will fail while he remains sedated
Wrong - no focal signs; the temporal link with the dose increase points to the drug
Correct - the sedating anticholinergic drug is the likely cause and should be withdrawn
Wrong - treating a side effect with a new drug is a prescribing cascade

mcq.stem:
A 78-year-old man with type 2 diabetes is bedbound after a hip fracture repair. You plan DVT prevention. His foot pulses are absent, the ankle-brachial pressure index is 0.6 and he has dry shiny skin on both shins.
Which DVT-prevention measure should be avoided?
mcq.e: Compression stockings are contraindicated in significant peripheral arterial disease (ABPI below about 0.8) because they reduce arterial inflow and can cause skin necrosis. Other contraindications include severe neuropathy, fragile skin and severe leg oedema from heart failure.
w: Correct - ABPI 0.6 means peripheral arterial disease; stockings can cause ischaemic necrosis
Wrong - leg exercises are safe and help venous return
Wrong - hydration is safe and reduces blood viscosity
Wrong - early mobilisation is the best DVT prevention
Wrong - turning prevents pressure injury and is safe

mcq.stem:
A 58-year-old woman, para 4, attends the Klinik Kesihatan complaining of leaking small amounts of urine when she coughs, laughs or lifts her grandchild. She has no urgency, no nocturia, and empties her bladder fully. Urinalysis is normal.
What type of incontinence is most likely?
mcq.e: Leakage of small amounts with raised intra-abdominal pressure, without urgency, points to stress incontinence from pelvic floor weakness or a poor urethral sphincter. Multiparity is a key risk factor. Mixed incontinence requires urge symptoms too.
w: Wrong - urge incontinence features a sudden overwhelming need to void
Wrong - overflow causes constant dribbling from incomplete emptying
Wrong - functional incontinence occurs with normal bladder function but barriers to the toilet
Wrong - no urge symptoms, so it is not mixed
Correct - small leaks with coughing, laughing and lifting are classic stress incontinence

mcq.stem:
A 62-year-old woman has leaked urine on sneezing and jogging for a year. There is no urgency. Pelvic examination shows good pelvic floor contraction and no prolapse; urinalysis is normal. She is keen to avoid surgery.
What is the most appropriate first-line treatment?
o: Oxybutynin 2.5 mg twice daily for 3 months
Pelvic floor muscle training for at least 3 months
Bladder retraining with timed voiding for 6 weeks
Referral for a mid-urethral sling operation
mcq.e: Pelvic floor (Kegel) exercises are first-line for stress incontinence and help 50-80%; give a full trial of at least 3 months. Antimuscarinics are ineffective for stress incontinence, bladder training targets urge incontinence, and surgery is reserved for failed conservative treatment.
w: Wrong - antimuscarinics treat urge, not stress incontinence
Correct - supervised pelvic floor training for at least 3 months is first-line
Wrong - bladder drill is the first-line behavioural treatment for urge incontinence
Wrong - surgery is reserved for failure of conservative therapy
Wrong - catheters carry infection risk and are not a treatment for stress leakage

mcq.stem:
An 83-year-old woman with mild Alzheimer's disease on donepezil has urgency and urge leakage. Urine culture is negative and post-void residual is 30 mL. Bladder training has helped only partly. Her daughter asks for medication.
Which drug is most likely to worsen her cognition?
mcq.e: Oxybutynin is a strongly anticholinergic, lipophilic drug that crosses the blood-brain barrier, causing confusion and delirium, and it directly opposes donepezil. It is on the Beers list for older adults. Mirabegron, a beta-3 agonist, is the preferred drug if one is needed.
w: Wrong - mirabegron is not anticholinergic; check BP before use
Wrong - topical oestrogen helps atrophic symptoms without cognitive effects
Wrong - lactulose treats constipation and has no anticholinergic action
Wrong - paracetamol is safe for cognition
Correct - oxybutynin is highly anticholinergic and antagonises donepezil

mcq.stem:
A 76-year-old man with known prostate enlargement has had constant dribbling of urine for 2 weeks, since starting an over-the-counter cold remedy containing chlorpheniramine. A smooth tender mass rises out of the pelvis. Urine dipstick shows no nitrites.
Which investigation will best confirm the mechanism of his incontinence?
mcq.e: Constant dribbling with a palpable bladder in a man with BPH, after an anticholinergic drug, suggests overflow incontinence from retention. A bladder ultrasound for post-void residual confirms it quickly (over 200 mL is significant). Catheterise, stop the anticholinergic and refer to urology.
w: Wrong - urodynamics are a specialist test, not the first step
Wrong - cystoscopy assesses the bladder lining, not emptying
Correct - a high PVR confirms retention with overflow
Wrong - PSA does not show retention and may be raised by it
Wrong - cytology is for suspected urothelial cancer, not overflow

mcq.stem:
An 88-year-old woman with severe knee osteoarthritis and mild dementia wets herself most nights before she reaches the toilet, which is at the far end of the house. She has no urgency or dysuria. Urinalysis is normal and post-void residual is 40 mL.
What is the most appropriate management?
o: Bedside commode and prompted voiding schedule
Pelvic floor muscle training for 3 months
Refer for urodynamic studies at the hospital
mcq.e: Leakage despite normal bladder function because the patient cannot reach the toilet in time is functional incontinence. Management removes the barrier: bedside commode, clear lit path, easy clothing and prompted voiding by caregivers. Drugs and pelvic floor exercises do not address the cause.
w: Wrong - the bladder is normal; an anticholinergic would worsen her dementia
Correct - remove the barrier with a commode and prompted voiding
Wrong - there is no stress leakage to treat
Wrong - catheters carry infection risk and are a last resort
Wrong - bladder function is already shown to be normal

mcq.stem:
An 80-year-old woman has had new urinary leakage and frequency for 3 weeks. She has had no bowel opening for 6 days and takes codeine for back pain. Abdomen is soft with a palpable sigmoid colon. Rectal examination reveals a rectum loaded with hard stool. Urinalysis is normal.
What is the most appropriate next step?
o: Clear the impaction and give regular laxatives
mcq.e: Stool impaction is a reversible cause of incontinence (the S in DIAPPERS); the loaded rectum presses on the bladder and urethra. Treat the impaction, review the codeine and prevent recurrence with laxatives before labelling a chronic type of incontinence.
w: Wrong - antimuscarinics worsen constipation and miss the reversible cause
Wrong - investigate only if leakage persists after treating impaction
Wrong - no prolapse found; the cause is bowel loading
Correct - treat the reversible cause first
Wrong - exercises do not address a loaded rectum

mcq.stem:
A 74-year-old woman with urge incontinence has not improved after 8 weeks of bladder training. You consider an antimuscarinic. Her past history includes hypertension, type 2 diabetes and knee osteoarthritis. Post-void residual is 40 mL.
Which additional finding would most clearly contraindicate an antimuscarinic?
mcq.e: Antimuscarinics dilate the pupil and can precipitate acute angle closure, so untreated angle-closure glaucoma is a contraindication. Other contraindications are urinary retention (high PVR), severe constipation and gastric retention. Controlled hypertension and diabetes are not barriers.
w: Correct - antimuscarinics can precipitate acute angle-closure glaucoma
Wrong - mild CKD only needs dose awareness
Wrong - reasonable glycaemic control is not a contraindication
Wrong - controlled BP does not affect antimuscarinic use (it matters more for mirabegron)
Wrong - knee effusion is irrelevant to antimuscarinic safety

mcq.stem:
A 55-year-old woman completes the QUID questionnaire at the Klinik Kesihatan. Her stress subscale score (questions 1-3) is 9 and her urge subscale score (questions 4-6) is 3.
What does this result suggest?
mcq.e: On the QUID, a stress score of 4 or more indicates stress incontinence and an urge score of 6 or more indicates urge incontinence. A stress score of 9 with an urge score of 3 meets only the stress threshold. Questionnaires support but do not replace history and examination.
w: Correct - stress score ≥4 with urge score below 6
Wrong - urge score of 3 is below the cut-off of 6
Wrong - mixed requires both thresholds to be met
Wrong - QUID does not assess overflow
Wrong - the stress score clearly exceeds its threshold

mcq.stem:
A 67-year-old woman with urinary leakage completes the UDI-6 in clinic. The total of her six item scores is 9 (maximum possible 18).
How should her symptom distress be categorised?
mcq.e: UDI-6 score = total ÷ 18 × 100, so 9 ÷ 18 × 100 = 50. The bands are 0-19 minimal, 20-39 mild, 40-59 moderate, 60-79 severe and 80-100 very severe. A score of 50 is moderate distress.
w: Wrong - minimal is 0-19
Wrong - mild is 20-39
Wrong - severe is 60-79
Wrong - very severe is 80-100
Correct - 9/18 × 100 = 50, within the moderate band 40-59

mcq.stem:
A 72-year-old woman reports a sudden overwhelming need to void, with leakage before reaching the toilet, frequency every hour and nocturia twice. She drinks six cups of coffee a day. Urinalysis is normal and post-void residual is 20 mL.
What is the most appropriate initial management?
o: Refer for a mid-urethral sling procedure
mcq.e: Urge incontinence is first managed behaviourally: reduce caffeine and alcohol and use bladder retraining, gradually lengthening voiding intervals until continent for 3-4 hours. Antimuscarinics are added if this fails, and neuromodulation is for refractory cases.
w: Wrong - drugs are second-line after behavioural therapy
Wrong - neuromodulation is for refractory urge incontinence
Wrong - slings treat stress, not urge incontinence
Correct - behavioural therapy is first-line for urge incontinence
Wrong - her PVR is normal; she empties well

mcq.stem:
A 74-year-old man with benign prostatic hyperplasia has overflow dribbling and two episodes of acute retention despite 6 months of tamsulosin and finasteride. Post-void residual is 380 mL. Renal function is normal and he is fit for anaesthesia.
Which procedure is most appropriate?
mcq.e: Overflow incontinence from prostatic obstruction that fails medical therapy is treated surgically with TURP (or laser/thermotherapy). Bladder neck suspension and slings are for female stress incontinence, and augmentation or neuromodulation are for refractory urge incontinence.
w: Wrong - bladder neck suspension treats female stress incontinence
Wrong - neuromodulation treats refractory urge incontinence
Correct - TURP relieves the obstruction causing overflow
Wrong - augmentation enlarges an overactive bladder; it would worsen retention
Wrong - tapes treat stress incontinence in women

mcq.stem:
A 79-year-old woman has urgency, frequency and burning on voiding for months. Three urine cultures have been negative. Speculum examination shows pale, thin, dry vaginal mucosa with petechiae and loss of rugae. Post-void residual is 25 mL.
What is the most appropriate treatment?
mcq.e: Atrophic urethritis and vaginitis (the A in DIAPPERS) from oestrogen deficiency cause urgency, dysuria and recurrent symptoms with sterile urine. Low-dose topical vaginal oestrogen is effective and safe. Repeated antibiotics without infection, and anticholinergics, are inappropriate.
w: Wrong - cultures are negative; antibiotics will not help
Correct - topical oestrogen treats atrophic urethritis
Wrong - treat the reversible cause before an anticholinergic
Wrong - systemic HRT carries more risk and is not needed
Wrong - drug treatment of urgency should follow correction of the reversible cause

mcq.stem:
A 78-year-old woman attends the Klinik Kesihatan for her BSSK-WE review. She lives with her son, walks without an aid and is independent in all daily activities. She had no falls this year. On the Timed Up and Go test, wearing her usual sandals, she takes 15 seconds.
How should this result be interpreted?
o: Normal mobility with no increase in falls risk
Independent mobility but at increased risk of falls
High falls risk and dependent on others for all mobility
Invalid result because she wore her own footwear
mcq.e: On the slide's bands, 10-20 s indicates good, independent mobility, but an older adult taking 12 s or more is considered at risk of falls. She is therefore independent yet at increased risk and needs further evaluation and targeted prevention. Patients should wear their regular footwear and may use their usual aid.
w: Wrong - normal is under 10 s, and 12 s or more already flags falls risk
Wrong - needing assistance corresponds to 20-30 s
Correct - 15 s is in the independent band but above the 12 s falls-risk cut-off
Wrong - high risk and dependence correspond to more than 30 s
Wrong - the test is meant to be done in regular footwear

mcq.stem:
An 80-year-old man has had two falls in a month, both soon after getting out of bed, preceded by light-headedness. He takes doxazosin 4 mg and amlodipine 10 mg for hypertension. BP lying is 142/80 mmHg; after 3 minutes standing it is 118/72 mmHg with dizziness. ECG shows sinus rhythm.
What is the most appropriate next step?
o: Taper and stop the doxazosin, then recheck postural BP
Increase amlodipine to control the lying blood pressure
Start fludrocortisone and continue current antihypertensives
Refer for a tilt-table test before changing any medicine
Advise bed rest until the dizziness settles completely
mcq.e: A systolic fall of 24 mmHg on standing (20 or more, or diastolic 10 or more, within 3 minutes) confirms orthostatic hypotension. Alpha-blockers are a classic cause in older adults and are on the potentially inappropriate list. Removing the offending drug comes before adding drugs or arranging specialist tests.
w: Correct - the alpha-blocker is the likely cause of orthostatic hypotension and should be withdrawn
Wrong - more vasodilation will worsen the postural drop
Wrong - adding a drug to treat a drug side effect is a prescribing cascade
Wrong - the diagnosis is already made at the bedside
Wrong - bed rest causes deconditioning and worsens orthostatic intolerance

mcq.stem:
A 76-year-old retired lorry driver reports two brief blackouts in 3 months. Both happened while shaving his neck and turning his head sharply to one side; he fell and recovered fully within seconds, with no confusion afterwards. Lying and standing BP are normal and the resting ECG is normal.
What is the most likely cause of his falls?
mcq.e: Syncope triggered by head turning or neck pressure (shaving, tight collar) suggests carotid sinus hypersensitivity, a cause of unexplained falls in older men. Falls on rising suggest postural hypotension, on leaving the toilet suggest vasovagal, and mid-walk suggest arrhythmia. Refer for carotid sinus massage testing under monitoring.
w: Wrong - postural BP is normal and the trigger was head turning, not standing
Wrong - vasovagal syncope typically follows micturition, defecation, pain or prolonged standing
Wrong - arrhythmia typically causes falls in the middle of walking, without a positional trigger
Wrong - rapid full recovery without confusion argues against a seizure
Correct - neck pressure and head turning are the classic triggers

mcq.stem:
A 74-year-old woman is brought in after being found on the bathroom floor by her husband. He saw her stiffen and jerk all four limbs for about 2 minutes. She had wet herself, has a bitten lateral tongue and remained confused for 40 minutes afterwards. Capillary glucose is 6.2 mmol/L.
What is the most likely cause of this fall?
o: Mechanical slip on a wet floor
mcq.e: Prolonged limb jerking, incontinence, lateral tongue biting and post-ictal confusion lasting many minutes point to a seizure. Syncope causes brief loss of consciousness with rapid full recovery, though a few jerks may occur. A new seizure in an older adult needs neuroimaging to look for stroke, tumour or subdural haematoma.
w: Wrong - syncope recovers within seconds to a minute, not 40 minutes of confusion
Correct - prolonged jerking, tongue biting and post-ictal confusion indicate a seizure
Wrong - postural syncope recovers rapidly once the patient is flat
Wrong - a mechanical slip does not cause jerking or post-ictal confusion
Wrong - cardiac syncope is brief with rapid recovery and pallor

mcq.stem:
An 84-year-old widow who lives alone is found by her neighbour on the kitchen floor. She fell during the night and could not get up, lying there for about 12 hours. She is alert, has no obvious fracture and wants to stay home. Her urine is dark brown.
Which investigation is most urgent?
mcq.e: A long lie (over 1 hour) risks rhabdomyolysis, which releases myoglobin (dark urine) and can cause acute kidney injury and hyperkalaemia. Creatine kinase, renal function and electrolytes are the urgent tests, and she needs hospital assessment. Other causes of the fall can be explored once she is safe.
w: Wrong - thyroid disease may contribute to falls but is not urgent here
Wrong - B12 is part of the falls work-up but does not address the immediate danger
Wrong - bone density is a later osteoporosis assessment
Correct - dark urine after a long lie suggests rhabdomyolysis with risk of acute kidney injury
Wrong - there is no history suggesting a seizure

mcq.stem:
You are reviewing five patients aged over 70 at a Klinik Kesihatan diabetes clinic. Each is asked about falls in the past year and observed walking.
Which patient meets the criteria for a multifactorial falls evaluation?
o: No falls, steady gait and TUG of 8 seconds
One trip on a wet floor, steady gait, TUG 9 seconds
No falls, but worried about falling, TUG 10 seconds
One fall at home and now feels unsteady on walking
No falls, uses reading glasses, TUG of 9 seconds
mcq.e: Further evaluation is indicated after two or more falls, one fall with unsteadiness, difficulty with gait or balance, or any fall needing medical attention. A single fall with a steady gait warrants advice and annual rescreening rather than a full multifactorial assessment.
w: Wrong - no falls and a normal TUG need only annual screening
Wrong - a single fall with normal gait and TUG does not meet the criteria
Wrong - fear of falling deserves attention, but with a normal TUG it does not meet the criteria
Correct - one fall plus unsteadiness is an indication for full evaluation
Wrong - corrected vision with a normal TUG does not trigger evaluation

mcq.stem:
A 79-year-old woman has had three falls in 6 months, usually when getting up at night. She feels drowsy in the mornings. Her medicines are amlodipine 5 mg, metformin 500 mg twice daily, atorvastatin 20 mg, omeprazole 20 mg and diazepam 5 mg at night, taken for 10 years. Postural BP and glucose are normal.
Which medication change is most likely to reduce her falls?
o: Stop the atorvastatin to prevent muscle weakness
Gradually taper and stop the nightly diazepam
Stop the omeprazole to improve calcium absorption
Switch metformin to glibenclamide once daily
Reduce amlodipine to 2.5 mg at night only
mcq.e: Long-acting benzodiazepines such as diazepam accumulate in older people, causing sedation, slowed reactions and ataxia, and are a leading drug cause of falls. After long-term use the dose must be tapered slowly to avoid withdrawal. Her postural BP and glucose are normal, so other drugs are less likely culprits.
w: Wrong - she has no myopathy symptoms; statins are not a major falls risk
Correct - a long-acting sedative causing morning drowsiness is the main modifiable cause
Wrong - long-term PPI has bone effects but does not explain recurrent night-time falls
Wrong - glibenclamide causes prolonged hypoglycaemia and would increase falls
Wrong - her postural BP is normal, so amlodipine is not the cause

mcq.stem:
An 86-year-old housebound woman has fallen twice this year. She rarely goes outdoors and wears a long telekung and covered clothing. Serum 25-hydroxyvitamin D is 22 nmol/L, calcium is normal and eGFR is 58. You plan a targeted intervention.
What is the most appropriate supplementation?
o: Daily cholecalciferol 800-1000 IU with adequate calcium
A single yearly oral dose of 500,000 IU vitamin D
Calcium carbonate 1.2 g daily without any vitamin D
Oral alendronate 70 mg weekly with no vitamin D replacement
mcq.e: Vitamin D supplementation in deficient or housebound older adults is a targeted falls-prevention measure, given as regular daily (or weekly) dosing with adequate calcium. Very large annual boluses have been linked to more falls and fractures. Bisphosphonates should not be started while vitamin D is deficient.
w: Correct - regular moderate-dose vitamin D with calcium suits a deficient housebound patient
Wrong - very high annual bolus doses were associated with increased falls
Wrong - calcium alone does not correct deficiency or improve muscle function
Wrong - correct vitamin D first; bisphosphonates can cause hypocalcaemia if deficient
Wrong - calcitriol risks hypercalcaemia and is reserved for advanced CKD

mcq.stem:
An 82-year-old man fell twice at night on the way to the toilet. His house has dim corridors, a loose rug in the hallway and no rails in the bathroom. Gait is slightly slow but steady, and postural BP is normal. His wife asks what will help most.
What is the most appropriate intervention?
o: Bed rails at night to stop him getting up alone
A sleeping tablet so he does not wake to pass urine
An indwelling urinary catheter to avoid night-time toilet trips
Restrict all fluids after midday to prevent nocturia
Home hazard assessment with lighting, rails and rug removal
mcq.e: Environmental hazards are a modifiable falls risk, and home hazard modification by an occupational therapist reduces falls in those with previous falls. Good lighting, removing rugs and fitting grab rails address his specific hazards. Restraints, sedatives and catheters all increase harm.
w: Wrong - bed rails cause falls from greater height and entrapment
Wrong - hypnotics increase falls and confusion
Wrong - catheters cause infection and reduce mobility
Wrong - severe fluid restriction risks dehydration, constipation and postural hypotension
Correct - modifying the identified hazards targets the cause of his falls

mcq.stem:
A 79-year-old man fell after briefly blacking out while climbing stairs. He has had exertional breathlessness for 3 months. Examination shows a slow-rising pulse and a harsh ejection systolic murmur radiating to the carotids. BP lying and standing is 118/80 mmHg. ECG shows left ventricular hypertrophy.
Which investigation is most appropriate?
mcq.e: Exertional syncope with a slow-rising pulse and an ejection systolic murmur radiating to the carotids suggests severe aortic stenosis. Echocardiography confirms valve severity and guides urgent cardiology referral. ECG and echo are the falls investigations for a suspected cardiac cause.
w: Wrong - there are no head injury or focal neurological features
Wrong - nothing suggests a seizure
Correct - an echo assesses suspected aortic stenosis causing exertional syncope
Wrong - neck imaging does not explain exertional syncope
Wrong - the murmur radiates to the carotids; it is not carotid disease

mcq.stem:
A 75-year-old man with type 2 diabetes on metformin 1 g twice daily for 12 years has fallen three times. He reports numb feet and unsteadiness in the dark. Examination shows reduced vibration and joint-position sense in both feet and a positive Romberg test. FBC shows MCV 106 fL.
Which blood test is most likely to reveal a treatable cause?
mcq.e: Long-term metformin reduces vitamin B12 absorption. B12 deficiency causes macrocytosis and a dorsal column and peripheral neuropathy with sensory ataxia, a treatable cause of falls. B12 is checked in the falls work-up when there are neurological abnormalities.
w: Correct - metformin-related B12 deficiency explains the macrocytosis and sensory ataxia
Wrong - hypothyroidism can raise MCV but does not cause dorsal column loss
Wrong - bone profile looks for bone pathology, not sensory ataxia
Wrong - lipids do not explain his neuropathy or falls
Wrong - CK is checked after a long lie, not for sensory ataxia

mcq.stem:
A 66-year-old man attends the Klinik Kesihatan for routine hypertension follow-up. He has never fallen, walks briskly and has no dizziness. He asks how often his doctor will check his risk of falling.
According to the AGS/BGS guideline on the slides, how often should he be screened?
mcq.e: The AGS/BGS guideline recommends screening all adults aged 65 and over for falls risk every year, by asking about falls in the past year and difficulty with walking or balance. Waiting for a fall misses the chance for prevention.
w: Wrong - screening aims to prevent the first fall
Wrong - 5-yearly screening is too infrequent
Correct - all adults aged 65 and over should be screened annually
Wrong - screening starts at 65, not 75
Wrong - many people at risk have no dizziness

mcq.stem:
A 77-year-old woman with one previous fall has a TUG of 14 seconds, mild quadriceps weakness and poor single-leg stance. She has no cardiac or neurological disease and her home has been made safe. She wants to reduce her chance of falling again.
Which exercise prescription has the best evidence?
o: Brisk walking alone for 20 minutes every day
Gentle stretching once a week at home
Avoid stairs and stay indoors where safe
Seated arm exercises with light weights
mcq.e: Individualised progressive strength and balance training (such as the Otago programme or tai chi), continued for at least 3 months, reduces falls in older adults. Walking alone does not improve balance enough and may increase exposure to falls in frail people. Activity restriction worsens deconditioning.
w: Wrong - walking alone does not train balance and is not enough
Wrong - stretching once a week is too little to change strength or balance
Wrong - restricting activity causes deconditioning and more falls
Wrong - upper-limb exercise does not address leg weakness or balance
Correct - progressive lower-limb strength and balance work reduces falls

mcq.stem:
An 84-year-old man with mild Alzheimer's disease, usually calm and conversant, has become much more muddled over 2 days. He is worse at night, pulls at his clothes and cannot keep his attention on a conversation. His temperature is 38.1 °C and urine dipstick shows leucocytes and nitrites.
What is the most likely explanation for his deterioration?
mcq.e: An acute change over days, fluctuation and inattention indicate delirium, and dementia is its strongest risk factor. Here a UTI is the likely precipitant. Labelling the change as dementia progression or sundowning misses a treatable and dangerous illness.
w: Wrong - dementia progresses over months to years, not 2 days
Correct - acute fluctuating inattention with fever is delirium on a background of dementia
Wrong - depression does not cause acute inattention with fever
Wrong - he has an established Alzheimer's diagnosis and an acute infective trigger
Wrong - fever and acute decline mean an illness must be sought

mcq.stem:
A medical officer assesses an 81-year-old woman whose daughter reports confusion that started yesterday and comes and goes. The officer applies the Confusion Assessment Method (CAM).
Apart from acute onset with a fluctuating course, which feature must be present for a positive CAM?
mcq.e: CAM requires feature 1 (acute onset and fluctuating course) AND feature 2 (inattention), plus EITHER feature 3 (disorganised thinking) OR feature 4 (altered consciousness). Inattention is the core of delirium; memory loss alone suggests dementia, and hallucinations are common but not required.
w: Wrong - hallucinations are common in delirium but not a CAM criterion
Wrong - disorganised thinking is one of two alternatives, not mandatory
Wrong - altered consciousness is the other alternative, not mandatory
Correct - inattention is required in every positive CAM
Wrong - memory loss is not specific to delirium

mcq.stem:
An 86-year-old woman is cared for at home by her daughter. Over 2 days she has become restless, shouting at night and not recognising her daughter. She has dysuria and a temperature of 37.9 °C; urine dipstick shows nitrites. She is drinking and has no focal signs. Her daughter asks for a strong sleeping pill.
What is the most appropriate management?
o: Prescribe lorazepam 1 mg at night for agitation
Advise the family to restrain her in bed at night
Start regular haloperidol 5 mg three times daily
Refer urgently to psychiatry for admission
Treat the UTI, reorientate and keep family close
mcq.e: The treatment of delirium is finding and treating the cause, here a UTI, plus non-drug measures: reorientation, familiar faces, glasses and hearing aids, hydration and good sleep routine. Benzodiazepines worsen delirium (except in alcohol withdrawal). Low-dose haloperidol is a short-term last resort for severe distress or danger.
w: Wrong - benzodiazepines worsen delirium and increase falls
Wrong - restraints increase agitation, injury and pressure damage
Wrong - regular high-dose antipsychotics are inappropriate; only low-dose short-term if essential
Wrong - delirium is a medical problem; treat the cause first
Correct - treating the cause with supportive non-drug care is the core of delirium management

mcq.stem:
A 72-year-old retired teacher has complained for 3 months that her memory is poor. She sleeps badly, has lost interest in her grandchildren and cries easily since her husband died 5 months ago. In testing she often says 'I don't know' and gives up quickly. Her GDS-15 score is 10.
What is the most likely diagnosis?
o: Alzheimer's disease in its early stage
mcq.e: Mood symptoms that precede the memory complaint, a patient who herself complains of poor memory, 'don't know' answers with poor effort, and a high GDS score point to depression mimicking dementia (pseudodementia). It is treatable, and cognition usually improves with treatment of the depression.
w: Correct - depression with cognitive complaints and a positive GDS-15 (5 or more)
Wrong - in Alzheimer's the family usually notices memory loss and the patient tends to minimise it
Wrong - nothing suggests an acute fluctuating course
Wrong - there are no vascular risk events or stepwise decline
Wrong - frontotemporal dementia presents with behaviour or language change

mcq.stem:
A 70-year-old man worried about his memory is assessed with the MoCA at a Klinik Kesihatan. He left school after 9 years of education. His raw MoCA score is 25 out of 30.
How should his result be interpreted?
mcq.e: On the MoCA one point is added if the person has 12 years of education or less, so his score becomes 26. The bands are 26-30 normal, 18-25 mild, 10-17 moderate and under 10 severe impairment. Forgetting the education adjustment would wrongly label him with mild cognitive impairment.
w: Wrong - this ignores the education point; 25 becomes 26
Wrong - moderate is 10-17
Wrong - severe is below 10
Correct - 25 plus 1 point for 9 years of education gives 26, in the normal band
Wrong - the MoCA is valid; the adjustment corrects for education

mcq.stem:
A 78-year-old woman is screened with the Elderly Cognitive Assessment Questionnaire (ECAQ) during her BSSK-WE visit. Her family say she has been getting lost in her own taman over the past year. She scores 3 out of 10.
How should this result be interpreted?
o: Borderline impairment, rescreen in a year
Result invalid because she has low education
mcq.e: On the ECAQ (maximum 10), scores of 4 or less indicate possible dementia, 5-6 borderline impairment and 7 or more normal. A score of 3 with functional decline needs a full dementia assessment including history, examination, bloods for reversible causes and imaging. The ECAQ was designed to reduce educational bias.
w: Wrong - normal is 7 or more
Correct - a score of 3 falls in the possible dementia range
Wrong - borderline is 5-6
Wrong - the ECAQ was designed for Asian elderly with less educational bias
Wrong - the ECAQ is not a depression scale

mcq.stem:
An 80-year-old man with Alzheimer's disease started donepezil 5 mg 6 weeks ago. He has since had two falls with dizziness and one brief faint. His pulse is regular at 44/min and BP is 118/70 mmHg. He takes no other rate-limiting drugs.
What is the most appropriate next step?
o: Increase donepezil to 10 mg for better effect
Do an ECG and withhold the donepezil
Prescribe a walking frame and review in 3 months
Start low-dose atropine tablets twice daily
mcq.e: Cholinesterase inhibitors increase vagal tone and can cause bradycardia, heart block and syncope, leading to falls. Check a pulse and ECG before and after starting. Withhold the drug and look for conduction disease; do not add drugs to counter the side effect.
w: Wrong - a higher dose would worsen the bradycardia
Wrong - adding a drug ignores the dangerous side effect
Correct - symptomatic bradycardia needs an ECG and withdrawal of the cholinesterase inhibitor
Wrong - a walking aid does not treat drug-induced syncope
Wrong - treating a side effect with another drug is a prescribing cascade

mcq.stem:
A 76-year-old woman is brought by her son because of slowly worsening forgetfulness over a year. She also reports constipation, weight gain, hoarse voice and feeling cold all the time. Pulse is 54/min, her skin is dry and ankle reflexes relax slowly. ECAQ is 6 out of 10.
Which investigation is most likely to reveal a reversible cause?
mcq.e: Before diagnosing dementia, exclude reversible causes such as hypothyroidism, B12 deficiency, depression, drugs, normal pressure hydrocephalus and subdural haematoma. Bradycardia, cold intolerance, weight gain, dry skin and slow-relaxing reflexes strongly suggest hypothyroidism, so a TFT is the key test.
w: Correct - the clinical features point to hypothyroidism, a reversible cause of cognitive decline
Wrong - EEG is for suspected seizures or encephalopathy
Wrong - lumbar puncture is a specialist test for atypical or rapid dementia
Wrong - amyloid imaging is a research or specialist tool, not primary care
Wrong - genotyping does not diagnose dementia or change management

mcq.stem:
A 74-year-old man has had 6 months of a slow, broad-based, shuffling gait in which his feet seem stuck to the floor, urinary urgency with incontinence, and increasing forgetfulness and apathy. There is no tremor or rigidity in the arms. B12 and thyroid function are normal.
Which investigation is most appropriate next?
o: Repeat serum vitamin B12 in 3 months
Nerve conduction studies of the legs
mcq.e: The triad of magnetic gait apraxia, urinary incontinence and cognitive decline suggests normal pressure hydrocephalus, a potentially reversible cause of dementia. Brain imaging shows ventricular enlargement out of proportion to atrophy, and neurosurgical referral may lead to a CSF shunt.
w: Wrong - B12 is already normal and does not explain the triad
Wrong - nothing suggests seizures
Correct - brain imaging looks for the ventriculomegaly of normal pressure hydrocephalus
Wrong - the incontinence is part of a neurological triad, not a primary bladder problem
Wrong - the gait is apraxic with preserved sensation, not neuropathic

mcq.stem:
A 79-year-old woman has a 2-year history of progressive memory loss and getting lost. She remains independent in personal care but needs help with finances. Bloods and CT brain exclude other causes and she is diagnosed with Alzheimer's disease. Her MMSE is 23/30, pulse 76/min and ECG normal.
Which drug is the most appropriate first-line treatment?
mcq.e: Acetylcholinesterase inhibitors such as donepezil are first-line for mild to moderate Alzheimer's disease; an MMSE of 23 indicates mild dementia. Memantine is used in moderate to severe disease or when cholinesterase inhibitors are not tolerated. Check pulse and ECG before starting because of bradycardia risk.
w: Wrong - memantine is for moderate to severe disease or AChEI intolerance
Wrong - antipsychotics do not treat cognition and raise stroke and death risk
Wrong - benzodiazepines worsen cognition and cause falls
Wrong - ginkgo has no proven benefit
Correct - a cholinesterase inhibitor is first-line for mild Alzheimer's disease

mcq.stem:
An 83-year-old man with moderate dementia has frightening visual hallucinations and has hit his wife twice despite treating his constipation and pain and a month of non-drug measures. The geriatric team suggest low-dose risperidone for a short period. His wife wants to know the main risk.
Which serious risk must be explained before starting it?
mcq.e: Antipsychotics in people with dementia increase the risk of stroke and death, as well as falls, sedation and parkinsonism. They are used only for severe distress or risk of harm after non-drug measures, at the lowest dose for the shortest time, with regular review. People with Lewy body dementia are especially sensitive.
w: Wrong - serious liver toxicity is not the key risk of risperidone
Wrong - agranulocytosis is the classic risk of clozapine
Wrong - lithium, not risperidone, causes hypothyroidism
Correct - antipsychotics raise stroke risk and mortality in dementia
Wrong - risperidone tends to cause weight gain and hyperglycaemia, not hypoglycaemia

mcq.stem:
A 68-year-old retired engineer is brought by his wife, who notices he struggles to plan trips, manage bills and follow recipes, which is new over a year. He scores 29/30 on the MMSE. Physical examination and bloods are normal.
What is the most appropriate next step in cognitive assessment?
o: Reassure him and repeat the MMSE in 2 years
Perform an ECAQ with his wife present
Reassure him as his score is above normal
mcq.e: The MMSE has a ceiling effect in well-educated people and poorly tests executive function. The MoCA is more sensitive for mild cognitive impairment because it tests executive and visuospatial skills (clock, cube, trail-making). A normal MMSE does not exclude early impairment when the history is convincing.
w: Wrong - a convincing history should not be dismissed
Correct - the MoCA detects executive and early impairment that the MMSE misses
Wrong - the AMT is a cruder screen with the same ceiling problem
Wrong - the ECAQ is a basic screen and will not detect subtle executive change
Wrong - the score is normal but the history suggests impairment

mcq.stem:
An 80-year-old woman went home 4 days after hip fracture surgery. Her daughter says she has become very quiet, sleeps most of the day and barely eats; the daughter thinks she is depressed. On review she is drowsy, drifts off mid-sentence and cannot name the months backwards, but is brighter in the evening. She is on regular codeine.
What is the most likely diagnosis?
mcq.e: Drowsiness, inattention and a fluctuating course arising acutely after surgery indicate delirium; the hypoactive form is the most often missed and mistaken for depression or tiredness. Opioids, pain, constipation and infection are likely precipitants. It carries a worse prognosis than hyperactive delirium.
w: Wrong - depression does not cause acute inattention and fluctuating drowsiness
Wrong - inattention and fluctuation are not normal post-operative recovery
Correct - acute, fluctuating inattention with drowsiness is hypoactive delirium
Wrong - there is no history of dementia and the change is acute
Wrong - an acute post-operative change with a clear trigger points to delirium

mcq.stem:
A 77-year-old woman with hypertension has been increasingly confused and unsteady for a week. Her doctor added hydrochlorothiazide 25 mg to her amlodipine 6 weeks ago. She has no fever and no focal neurology. Serum sodium is 119 mmol/L, potassium 3.2 mmol/L and glucose 6.0 mmol/L.
What is the most likely cause of her confusion?
mcq.e: Thiazides are a common cause of hyponatraemia in older women, often within weeks of starting, and a sodium of 119 mmol/L readily explains confusion and unsteadiness. Medication is a key precipitant of delirium. Stop the thiazide and arrange hospital correction if severe or symptomatic.
w: Correct - recent thiazide plus sodium 119 mmol/L explains the delirium
Wrong - the onset is acute and there is a clear metabolic cause
Wrong - hypothyroidism is gradual and does not explain a newly low sodium
Wrong - possible in falls, but the metabolic cause and timing fit better
Wrong - there is no documented hypotension, and the sodium explains it

mcq.stem:
A 78-year-old woman started amlodipine 10 mg for hypertension 4 months ago. She then developed ankle swelling and was given furosemide 40 mg daily. She now has urinary urgency and leakage, and potassium is 3.3 mmol/L. Heart and lungs are normal and urine dipstick is negative.
What is the most appropriate management?
o: Add oxybutynin 2.5 mg twice daily for the leakage
Increase furosemide and add potassium supplements
Add spironolactone to correct the hypokalaemia
Stop furosemide and switch amlodipine to another drug
Prescribe compression stockings and continue all drugs
mcq.e: This is a prescribing cascade: amlodipine caused dose-related ankle oedema, misread as fluid overload and treated with furosemide, which then caused urgency, incontinence and hypokalaemia. The fix is to remove the original culprit and the drug added for its side effect, not to add a third drug.
w: Wrong - adding an anticholinergic extends the cascade and risks confusion
Wrong - more diuretic worsens incontinence and electrolytes
Wrong - another drug does not address the cause
Correct - remove the drug causing the oedema and stop the unnecessary diuretic
Wrong - continuing the cascade leaves her incontinent and hypokalaemic

mcq.stem:
An 80-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes has had early-morning sweating and confusion three times this month; capillary glucose was 2.8 mmol/L at one episode. She takes glibenclamide 10 mg twice daily and metformin 500 mg twice daily. HbA1c is 6.1% and eGFR is 35 mL/min/1.73 m².
What is the most appropriate change to her treatment?
o: Increase metformin to 1 g twice daily
Keep the same regimen and add a bedtime snack
Switch to premixed insulin twice daily
Reduce glibenclamide to 5 mg twice daily
Stop glibenclamide and use a DPP-4 inhibitor
mcq.e: Glibenclamide is a long-acting sulfonylurea with renally cleared active metabolites that cause prolonged hypoglycaemia in older people with CKD; it is on the Beers list. With an HbA1c of 6.1% she is over-treated. Stop it and use a low-hypoglycaemia option such as a DPP-4 inhibitor (e.g. linagliptin), with relaxed targets.
w: Wrong - metformin should be limited to 1 g a day at eGFR 30-44
Wrong - a snack does not remove the cause of recurrent hypoglycaemia
Wrong - insulin adds hypoglycaemia risk and complexity in a patient already over-treated
Wrong - any dose of this long-acting sulfonylurea remains hazardous in CKD
Correct - remove the long-acting sulfonylurea and use a drug with low hypoglycaemia risk

mcq.stem:
An 86-year-old woman with atrial fibrillation has had nausea, anorexia and blurred vision with a yellow tinge for a week. She takes digoxin 0.25 mg daily and bisoprolol 2.5 mg. Pulse is irregular at 48/min. eGFR is 30 mL/min/1.73 m² and potassium is 3.1 mmol/L.
What is the most likely cause of her symptoms?
mcq.e: Digoxin is renally cleared, so reduced GFR leads to accumulation; doses above 0.125 mg/day in older people increase toxicity risk, and hypokalaemia worsens it. Nausea, anorexia, visual disturbance (yellow-green) and bradyarrhythmia are classic. Check a digoxin level, ECG and electrolytes and withhold the drug.
w: Wrong - gastroenteritis does not explain the visual change and slow AF
Wrong - cataracts cause gradual blurring, not acute yellow vision with nausea
Correct - high dose, poor renal function and hypokalaemia produce digoxin toxicity
Wrong - sick sinus does not cause nausea and xanthopsia
Wrong - hypothyroidism is gradual and does not cause yellow vision

mcq.stem:
A 78-year-old man with heart failure (ejection fraction 35%) and CKD with eGFR 38 mL/min/1.73 m² has painful knee osteoarthritis. He weighs 62 kg and has no liver disease. He asks for a stronger painkiller.
Which is the most appropriate first-line analgesic?
o: Oral diclofenac sodium 50 mg three times daily
Regular paracetamol 1 g four times daily
Oral ibuprofen 400 mg three times daily
mcq.e: NSAIDs, including COX-2 inhibitors, are a drug-disease interaction in CKD and heart failure: they worsen renal function and cause fluid retention. Regular paracetamol is first-line in older adults (reduce the dose if under 50 kg or with liver disease). Pethidine is avoided because its metabolite norpethidine accumulates and causes neurotoxicity.
w: Wrong - NSAIDs worsen renal function and heart failure
Correct - paracetamol is safe in CKD and heart failure at this weight
Wrong - COX-2 inhibitors carry the same renal and fluid-retention risks
Wrong - pethidine metabolites accumulate in CKD and cause seizures
Wrong - ibuprofen is also an NSAID with the same risks

mcq.stem:
An 83-year-old woman becomes confused, cannot pass urine and is constipated 3 days after buying an over-the-counter cough and cold syrup. The label lists several ingredients. She is afebrile and her chest is clear. A palpable bladder is found.
Which ingredient is most likely responsible?
mcq.e: First-generation antihistamines such as chlorpheniramine and diphenhydramine are strongly anticholinergic and sedating. In older people they cause confusion, urinary retention, constipation and falls, and are on the Beers list. Non-sedating antihistamines such as loratadine are preferred if an antihistamine is needed.
w: Correct - a sedating anticholinergic antihistamine explains confusion, retention and constipation
Wrong - paracetamol is not anticholinergic
Wrong - guaifenesin is an expectorant without anticholinergic effects
Wrong - bromhexine is a mucolytic and does not cause retention
Wrong - loratadine is non-sedating with minimal anticholinergic effect

mcq.stem:
An 80-year-old man attends with a bag of medicines from three hospital clinics and a private GP. He takes 11 regular drugs, including two NSAIDs, two PPIs and a sleeping tablet, and feels dizzy and tired. He is not sure why he takes several of them.
What is the most appropriate next step?
o: Give a weekly pill organiser and change nothing
Refer him back to each specialist to review their drugs
Do a structured review with STOPP/Beers and deprescribe
Stop all his medicines at once and restart one by one
Continue all drugs as each was prescribed by a doctor
mcq.e: Polypharmacy (here 11 drugs) with duplicates and symptoms calls for a structured brown-bag medication review using explicit criteria such as Beers or STOPP/START. Deprescribe drugs without an indication or with harms outweighing benefits, one at a time with tapering where needed, and coordinate care across prescribers.
w: Wrong - an organiser helps adherence but leaves duplicates and harmful drugs
Wrong - fragmented review by several clinics caused the problem
Correct - a structured review removes duplicates and inappropriate drugs
Wrong - abrupt cessation risks withdrawal and decompensation
Wrong - the duplicates and symptoms show the regimen needs review

mcq.stem:
A 78-year-old widow has had difficulty sleeping since her husband died a year ago. She takes 2 hours to fall asleep, naps in the afternoon and drinks coffee after dinner. She is not depressed on screening and asks for the diazepam her friend uses.
What is the most appropriate management?
o: Diazepam 5 mg at night for 3 months
Chlorpheniramine 4 mg at night when needed
Sleep hygiene and CBT for insomnia
mcq.e: Long-acting benzodiazepines such as diazepam should generally be avoided in the elderly because they accumulate and cause falls, confusion and dependence. Sedating antihistamines and tricyclics are anticholinergic, and Z-drugs carry similar falls risk. Sleep hygiene (no afternoon naps, no evening caffeine) and CBT for insomnia are first-line.
w: Wrong - a long-acting benzodiazepine causes falls and confusion in older people
Wrong - sedating antihistamines are anticholinergic and cause confusion and retention
Wrong - amitriptyline is anticholinergic, sedating and causes postural hypotension
Wrong - Z-drugs also increase falls and fractures
Correct - non-drug measures address her clear sleep-hygiene problems

mcq.stem:
A 76-year-old man with atrial fibrillation, hypertension and diabetes (CHA2DS2-VASc 4) takes aspirin 100 mg only, because a previous doctor felt he was 'too old' for anticoagulation. He walks unaided, has not fallen, and has eGFR 62 and no bleeding history.
What is the most appropriate change?
o: Continue aspirin alone because he is now over 75 years
Stop all antithrombotics due to his age
Switch to an oral anticoagulant such as apixaban
Add digoxin to control his heart rate
mcq.e: Omission of anticoagulation in atrial fibrillation is a classic START criterion. Age increases stroke risk more than bleeding risk, and aspirin gives little stroke protection in AF. A DOAC such as apixaban is preferred, with renal function and bleeding risk reviewed.
w: Wrong - aspirin is ineffective for stroke prevention in AF
Wrong - dual antiplatelets add bleeding without matching anticoagulant benefit
Wrong - age is a reason to anticoagulate, not to stop
Correct - an oral anticoagulant is indicated and was wrongly omitted
Wrong - rate control does not prevent stroke

mcq.stem:
A 79-year-old man with CKD (eGFR 28 mL/min/1.73 m²) has severe pain from vertebral metastases. During a hospital stay he was given repeated intramuscular doses of one analgesic and developed tremor, myoclonic jerks, agitation and a seizure.
Which analgesic should be avoided in older people because of this toxicity?
mcq.e: Pethidine (meperidine) is metabolised to norpethidine, which accumulates in renal impairment and causes neurotoxicity: tremor, myoclonus, agitation and seizures. It is listed as an analgesic to avoid in the elderly. Buprenorphine and fentanyl are less dependent on renal clearance.
w: Wrong - paracetamol does not cause neuroexcitation
Correct - the metabolite norpethidine accumulates in CKD and causes seizures
Wrong - topical NSAID has minimal systemic absorption and no neuroexcitation
Wrong - buprenorphine is relatively safe in renal impairment
Wrong - fentanyl is largely hepatically cleared and preferred in CKD

mcq.stem:
An 84-year-old woman with heart failure, diabetes, knee osteoarthritis, recurrent falls, mild cognitive impairment and 9 regular medicines has had three hospital admissions in a year. She lives with her daughter, who works full time and feels overwhelmed.
Which approach is most likely to reduce further admissions?
o: Comprehensive geriatric assessment by an MDT
Immediate admission to a private nursing home
Adding drugs to tighten each disease target
Annual review only at the Klinik Kesihatan
mcq.e: Comprehensive geriatric assessment evaluates medical, psychosocial and functional needs to build a coordinated, individualised plan with medication review and caregiver support. It reduces readmission, institutionalisation and functional decline in frail older people. Fragmented disease-by-disease care drives polypharmacy.
w: Correct - a coordinated multidisciplinary assessment and plan reduces admissions
Wrong - fragmented specialist care adds drugs and misses function and caregiver strain
Wrong - institutional care is not the first step and is not her wish
Wrong - tighter targets mean more drugs and more adverse events
Wrong - annual review is too infrequent for her needs

mcq.stem:
A 79-year-old woman attends for BSSK-WE screening with her son, who answers all questions. You notice bruises of different ages on both upper arms, poor hygiene and that she looks fearful. The son explains she is clumsy and says he manages her pension.
What is the most appropriate next step?
o: Accept the explanation and arrange a falls review
Confront the son about abuse in front of his mother
Interview her alone, document and refer to the MSW
Order a skeletal survey and review in 3 months
Advise the son to buy her a walking frame only
mcq.e: Bruises of different ages, fearfulness, poor hygiene and financial control by a caregiver raise suspicion of physical, financial and neglect forms of elder abuse, which BSSK-WE screens for. Speak to the patient alone, document findings carefully, assess safety and refer to the medical social worker and JKM.
w: Wrong - unexplained bruises in a fearful patient must not be accepted at face value
Wrong - confrontation may endanger the patient and prevent disclosure
Correct - private interview, documentation and social work referral protect the patient
Wrong - investigations alone delay safeguarding
Wrong - this ignores the warning signs of abuse

mcq.stem:
An 81-year-old man attends for BSSK-WE screening. His weight has fallen from 60 kg to 56 kg in 4 months, he has several missing teeth and loose dentures, and he lives alone. His calf circumference is reduced.
Which screening tool best quantifies his nutritional risk?
o: Barthel Index of activities of daily living
mcq.e: BSSK-WE includes anthropometry, dietary intake and oral health. Unintentional loss of over 5% of body weight in 6 months (here about 7%) is significant. The MNA-SF is a validated nutrition screen for older adults; positive results lead to dietitian and dental input and a search for causes such as depression or cancer.
w: Wrong - depression may contribute, but the GDS does not quantify nutrition
Wrong - the Braden scale assesses pressure ulcer risk
Wrong - the Barthel Index measures ADL dependency
Correct - the MNA-SF is designed to screen older people for malnutrition
Wrong - the Morse scale assesses inpatient falls risk

mcq.stem:
A 70-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes and COPD attends the Klinik Kesihatan for her BSSK-WE review. She asks which of her vaccinations needs to be repeated every year.
Which vaccine should be given annually?
mcq.e: Influenza vaccine is given every year because circulating strains change; older adults with diabetes or COPD are a priority group. Pneumococcal vaccination is a one-off or limited course, zoster vaccine is a two-dose course, and tetanus boosters are given about every 10 years.
w: Wrong - pneumococcal vaccine is not given annually
Wrong - tetanus boosters are about every 10 years
Wrong - recombinant zoster is a two-dose course, not yearly
Wrong - hepatitis B is not a routine annual booster
Correct - influenza vaccine is repeated every year

mcq.stem:
A 72-year-old woman completes BSSK-WE screening at a Klinik Kesihatan. She is asymptomatic, but the screen shows she has fallen once with unsteadiness this year and now needs help with bathing on the ADL section. Her BP and glucose are well controlled.
What is the most appropriate next step?
o: File the form and repeat the screen next year
Assess the positive domains and agree a care plan
Refer her directly to the hospital geriatric clinic
Start vitamin D and take no further action
Reassure her as her chronic diseases are controlled
mcq.e: Screening aims to detect problems early, prevent disability and maintain independence, which only happens if positive findings are acted on. A fall with unsteadiness and new ADL dependence need a falls and functional assessment in primary care with a targeted plan (physiotherapy, home safety, medication review) and follow-up.
w: Wrong - positive screens left unaddressed defeat the purpose of screening
Correct - positive domains need assessment and a targeted, followed-up plan
Wrong - most of this assessment can begin in primary care
Wrong - vitamin D alone does not address gait, home hazards or ADL support
Wrong - function and falls risk matter as much as disease control

mcq.stem:
An 82-year-old man lives with his wife. He washes, dresses, feeds and toilets himself without help. Over the past year his son has taken over his banking, drives him to appointments and does the heavy housework, and his wife now organises his medicines because he forgets them.
Which Clinical Frailty Scale level best describes him?
mcq.e: CFS 5 (mildly frail) describes people who need help with high-order instrumental activities such as finances, transport, heavy housework and medications, while personal care is intact. CFS 4 people are not dependent on others, and CFS 6 people need help with all outside activities and with bathing.
w: Wrong - CFS 3 people have controlled conditions and need no help
Wrong - CFS 4 people are slowed but not dependent on others
Wrong - CFS 7 means complete dependence for personal care
Correct - help with finances, transport, housework and medicines with intact personal care is CFS 5
Wrong - CFS 6 requires help with all outside activities and with bathing

mcq.stem:
A 70-year-old woman with metastatic pancreatic cancer has an estimated life expectancy of about 3 months. Until now she has remained independent: she cooks, shops and walks to the market each day with no help.
Which Clinical Frailty Scale level should be recorded?
mcq.e: CFS 9 (terminally ill) is used for people approaching the end of life with a life expectancy under 6 months who are not otherwise evidently frail. It is the exception on the scale, because it is based on prognosis rather than on function. CFS 8 people are completely dependent and approaching end of life.
w: Correct - a life expectancy under 6 months defines CFS 9 even if function is preserved
Wrong - her terminal illness overrides her current fitness
Wrong - CFS 3 does not account for her limited prognosis
Wrong - CFS 4 describes being slowed up, not terminal illness
Wrong - CFS 8 requires complete dependence for personal care

mcq.stem:
A 78-year-old woman is assessed with the Fried frailty phenotype. She has unintentionally lost 5 kg in the past year and her timed 4-metre walk is slow. She denies exhaustion, her grip strength is normal for her sex and BMI, and she gardens for an hour every day.
How should she be classified?
mcq.e: The Fried phenotype has five criteria: unintentional weight loss, exhaustion, weakness (grip), slow walking speed and low physical activity. She meets two (weight loss and slow gait). One or two criteria indicate pre-frailty, three or more frailty. Pre-frailty is the best window for reversing decline.
w: Wrong - robust means none of the five criteria
Wrong - frailty requires 3 or more criteria
Wrong - the Fried phenotype does not grade severe frailty
Wrong - the Fried phenotype is a stand-alone tool
Correct - two of five criteria indicate pre-frailty

mcq.stem:
An 80-year-old man has been admitted with pneumonia and is now bedbound and needs help with all personal care. His wife says that 2 weeks ago he walked to the mosque daily, managed his own affairs and had only well-controlled hypertension, though he did not exercise regularly.
Which CFS level should guide decisions about his treatment?
o: CFS 7, based on his current dependence
CFS 8, as he is acutely unwell and bedbound
CFS 3, based on his baseline before illness
CFS 5, as an average of before and now
CFS 9, as pneumonia may be life-limiting
mcq.e: The Clinical Frailty Scale should reflect baseline function about 2 weeks before the acute illness, using history from the patient and family. Scoring current acute dependence would wrongly label a robust man as severely frail and could lead to inappropriate limits on treatment.
w: Wrong - acute illness dependence should not be scored
Wrong - acute bedbound state is not his baseline
Correct - score the baseline from 2 weeks before admission
Wrong - there is no averaging; use baseline
Wrong - CFS 9 is for known life expectancy under 6 months

mcq.stem:
A 76-year-old woman is pre-frail: she has lost weight and her walking speed is slow, but she remains independent. She eats one small meal a day and spends most of the day seated. Bloods including vitamin D and thyroid function are normal.
Which intervention is most effective in reversing her frailty?
o: Advise rest to conserve her limited energy
Resistance exercise with adequate protein intake
High-dose vitamin E and multivitamin tablets
Early placement in a residential care home
mcq.e: Progressive resistance and balance exercise combined with adequate protein and energy intake is the most effective intervention to delay or reverse frailty, especially in the pre-frail stage. Medication review and treating underlying problems add to it. Rest accelerates sarcopenia.
w: Wrong - rest worsens sarcopenia and deconditioning
Correct - strength training plus protein is the core of frailty reversal
Wrong - hormone therapy is not recommended for frailty
Wrong - antioxidant supplements have no proven benefit
Wrong - she is independent; institutional care is unnecessary

mcq.stem:
A 79-year-old woman is assessed with the Katz Index at a community screening. She feeds herself, is continent, transfers from bed to chair alone and uses the toilet independently. She needs help to wash her back and legs and to put on her baju kurung and fasten buttons.
How should her Katz score be interpreted?
mcq.e: The Katz Index scores six functions yes/no: bathing, dressing, toileting, transferring, continence and feeding. She is independent in four and dependent in bathing and dressing, giving 4, which the slides classify as moderate impairment. Six is full function and 2 or less severe impairment.
w: Correct - independent in 4 of 6 functions is moderate impairment
Wrong - she needs help with bathing and dressing
Wrong - 2 or less means dependence in at least four functions
Wrong - she scores 4, and only 6 is full function
Wrong - she is independent in four functions, not three

mcq.stem:
A 70-year-old man is in a stroke rehabilitation unit. The physiotherapist wants a tool that grades the degree of help needed in each of ten activities, including stairs and ambulation, so she can track small weekly gains and plan discharge.
Which instrument is most suitable?
mcq.e: The Barthel Index has ten domains with graded scores, detecting finer changes during rehabilitation and informing discharge planning; it is widely used in stroke units. The Katz Index is a quick yes/no screen of six basic ADLs used in primary care and community screening.
w: Wrong - Katz uses yes/no scoring and is too coarse for small gains
Wrong - the Lawton scale measures instrumental, not basic, ADLs
Correct - graded scoring across ten domains tracks rehabilitation progress
Wrong - the MoCA assesses cognition
Wrong - the CFS grades overall frailty, not specific ADLs

mcq.stem:
An 83-year-old woman is assessed before discharge from a rehabilitation ward after a hip fracture. Her total Barthel Index score is 55 out of 100. Her family ask how much help she will need at home.
How is this score categorised?
mcq.e: On the 100-point Barthel Index, 0-20 is total dependency, 21-60 severe, 61-90 moderate, 91-99 slight and 100 independent. A score of 55 means severe dependency: she will need substantial daily help, which should shape the discharge and caregiver plan.
w: Wrong - total dependency is 0-20
Wrong - moderate dependency is 61-90
Wrong - slight dependency is 91-99
Correct - 55 falls in the severe dependency band of 21-60
Wrong - independent is 100

mcq.stem:
A 74-year-old retired clerk lives alone. Her niece notices that over 6 months she has repeatedly missed her pills and had her electricity cut off for unpaid bills. She still bathes, dresses and feeds herself well. ECAQ is 6 out of 10.
Which area of function is typically lost first in early cognitive decline?
mcq.e: Instrumental ADLs such as managing money, medications, transport and shopping need complex cognition and are lost before basic ADLs. The Lawton IADL scale detects this early decline. Among basic ADLs, bathing is usually lost first and feeding last.
w: Wrong - feeding is the last basic ADL to be lost
Wrong - continence is lost late
Wrong - transfers are a basic ADL lost later
Wrong - bathing is the first basic ADL lost, but IADLs go before it
Correct - instrumental activities such as finances are lost first

mcq.stem:
An 87-year-old man with advanced vascular dementia is losing function steadily. His daughter, who cares for him, asks which basic self-care activity he is likely to keep the longest.
Which activity is usually retained longest?
mcq.e: The Katz hierarchy describes the usual order of loss: bathing, dressing, toileting, transferring, continence and finally feeding. Recovery tends to occur in the reverse order. Knowing this helps caregivers anticipate needs and plan support.
w: Wrong - bathing is typically lost first
Correct - feeding is the last basic ADL to be lost
Wrong - dressing is lost early, after bathing
Wrong - toileting is lost before transferring and feeding
Wrong - transferring is lost before continence and feeding

mcq.stem:
A 72-year-old man has had gradually worsening hearing in both ears for several years. He struggles to follow conversation in noisy kenduri and cannot hear his granddaughter's high voice. Otoscopy is normal. Rinne is positive in both ears and Weber is central.
What is the most likely diagnosis?
mcq.e: Presbycusis is a gradual, bilateral, symmetrical sensorineural loss affecting high frequencies first, typically with difficulty in background noise. Normal otoscopy, positive Rinne bilaterally and central Weber fit symmetrical sensorineural loss. A pure-tone audiogram is the gold standard to confirm it.
w: Wrong - wax would be seen on otoscopy and gives conductive loss
Wrong - otosclerosis is conductive, so Rinne would be negative
Wrong - Ménière's causes episodic vertigo, tinnitus and fluctuating loss
Wrong - a vestibular schwannoma causes unilateral, asymmetric loss
Correct - gradual symmetrical high-frequency sensorineural loss in old age

mcq.stem:
A 68-year-old woman woke this morning with marked hearing loss in her left ear and tinnitus. She has no ear pain or discharge. Otoscopy is normal on both sides. Weber lateralises to the right ear and Rinne is positive on the left.
What is the most appropriate management?
o: Reassure and review her hearing in 1 month
Arrange ear syringing at the clinic
Refer for routine hearing aid fitting
mcq.e: Weber lateralising to the good ear with a positive Rinne on the affected side indicates sensorineural loss. Sudden sensorineural hearing loss is an ENT emergency: early corticosteroids improve recovery, and MRI is needed to exclude a vestibular schwannoma. Delay worsens the outcome.
w: Wrong - waiting reduces the chance of recovery with steroids
Wrong - the ear canal and drum are normal; drops have no role
Correct - sudden sensorineural loss needs urgent ENT assessment
Wrong - otoscopy shows no wax
Wrong - urgent treatment comes before rehabilitation

mcq.stem:
An 80-year-old man's wife says he has become hard of hearing over 2 months, mainly on the right. He has no pain, vertigo or discharge. Otoscopy shows the right ear canal fully occluded by hard brown material; the left drum is normal.
What is the most appropriate first step?
o: Soften and remove the wax, then reassess
Fit a hearing aid in the right ear
Refer routinely to ENT for assessment
Request an MRI of the internal auditory meatus
mcq.e: Cerumen impaction is a common reversible cause of conductive hearing loss in older people. Treat underlying physical obstructions first with softening drops then irrigation or microsuction, and reassess hearing afterwards. Audiometry and aids come after removing the obstruction.
w: Correct - remove the reversible obstruction before further assessment
Wrong - the aid would be blocked and the cause is treatable
Wrong - an audiogram through impacted wax will be misleading
Wrong - wax removal can be done in primary care
Wrong - the cause is visible; no imaging is needed

mcq.stem:
A 75-year-old woman completes the Hearing Handicap Inventory for the Elderly-Screening (HHIE-S) at her BSSK-WE visit. She answers 'yes' to most questions about avoiding social events and feeling embarrassed, giving a total of 28 out of 40.
What does this score indicate?
o: No handicap, so no referral is needed
Mild handicap, repeat screening in 5 years
Normal hearing for her age, reassure her
Significant handicap, refer to an audiologist
Moderate handicap, start ear drops now
mcq.e: On the HHIE-S (0-40), 0-8 indicates no handicap, 10-24 mild to moderate handicap and 26-40 significant handicap with referral to an audiologist recommended. A score of 28 needs audiological assessment and likely amplification.
w: Wrong - no handicap is 0-8
Wrong - mild to moderate is 10-24, and screening interval is not the issue
Wrong - the HHIE-S measures handicap, and 28 is high
Correct - 26-40 is significant handicap needing audiology referral
Wrong - ear drops do not treat hearing handicap

mcq.stem:
A 70-year-old man with type 2 diabetes keeps bumping into door frames on both sides. He has no eye pain and his central vision is 6/9 in each eye. Fundoscopy shows large, deeply cupped optic discs, and intraocular pressure is 28 mmHg in both eyes.
What is the most likely diagnosis?
mcq.e: Primary open-angle glaucoma causes painless, gradual peripheral field loss with preserved central acuity until late, enlarged optic disc cupping and often raised intraocular pressure. It is asymptomatic early, which is why older adults need regular eye screening. Refer to ophthalmology for treatment.
w: Wrong - cataract causes generalised blurring and glare, not peripheral loss with cupping
Correct - painless peripheral field loss, disc cupping and raised IOP
Wrong - AMD affects central vision
Wrong - maculopathy reduces central acuity
Wrong - detachment is sudden, with flashes, floaters and a curtain

mcq.stem:
A 78-year-old woman says straight lines such as door frames look wavy and there is a blurred patch in the centre of her vision when she reads the Quran. Peripheral vision is normal. Fundoscopy shows yellowish deposits at both maculae. She is not diabetic.
What is the most likely diagnosis?
mcq.e: Age-related macular degeneration causes central vision loss and distortion (metamorphopsia) with drusen at the macula, while peripheral vision is spared. Sudden distortion suggests wet AMD, which needs urgent ophthalmology referral for anti-VEGF treatment.
w: Correct - central distortion with macular drusen is AMD
Wrong - cataract causes overall blurring and glare without distortion
Wrong - glaucoma affects peripheral vision first
Wrong - detachment causes flashes, floaters and a field curtain
Wrong - she is not diabetic and the findings are drusen

mcq.stem:
A 72-year-old man has been bedbound since a stroke and needs help with all personal care. He has no family or heirs, no income and no home. A government medical officer has certified him as chronically ill. The hospital social worker is planning his long-term placement.
Which JKM facility is most appropriate?
mcq.e: Rumah Ehsan provides JKM residential care for elderly people who are frail, poor, without heirs and unable to care for themselves, certified chronically ill by a government medical officer. Rumah Seri Kenangan is for poor elderly without heirs who can still self-care.
w: Wrong - Rumah Seri Kenangan requires residents to be able to self-care
Wrong - PAWE is a day activity centre, not residential care
Correct - Rumah Ehsan is for frail elderly unable to self-care
Wrong - KWE is a community club
Wrong - KOSPEN Warga Emas is a community NCD prevention programme

mcq.stem:
A 68-year-old widow who lives alone in a rented room tells you she often skips meals because she cannot afford food. Her only household income is RM900 a month from odd jobs. She does not live in an institution and receives no other welfare aid.
Which scheme provides the monthly cash support she should be referred for?
mcq.e: Bantuan Warga Emas is JKM monthly cash assistance (RM600 a month from 2025) for people aged 60 and over with household income below the poverty line (RM2,589 a month on the slide), not in an institution and not receiving other aid. Refer through the medical social worker or JKM office.
w: Wrong - mySalam is takaful cover for critical illness, not monthly cash
Wrong - SMUE gives an annual voucher and funeral aid, not monthly support
Wrong - PEKA B40 provides health screening and device aid
Correct - BWE gives monthly cash to poor elderly aged 60 and over
Wrong - KBDR provides volunteer home help, not money

mcq.stem:
An 80-year-old widower lives alone in his own house and wants to stay there. He is cognitively intact but, since a knee replacement, struggles with cooking, cleaning and getting to hospital appointments. He has no family nearby and enough money for his basic needs.
Which programme best meets his needs?
mcq.e: Khidmat Bantu di Rumah is a volunteer-based home support service for elderly people living alone, helping with meals, housekeeping, bathing, companionship, medicines and hospital visits. It supports ageing in place, which is his wish, rather than institutional care.
w: Wrong - residential care is unnecessary and against his wishes
Wrong - he is not dependent for personal care
Wrong - PAWE offers activities at a centre, not help at home
Wrong - takaful does not provide practical home help
Correct - KBDR volunteers support elderly people living alone at home
